The resulting code uses finite elements to solve the mechanical problem and the boundary element method to solve the heat equation. Numerical validation shows good agreement with experimental data.

To understand the relationship between the topology of a Fermi surface, magnetic susceptibility, and superconducting properties, researchers use topological Weyl semi-metal materials as a study subject. By applying a magnetic field, researchers can control the topology of a Fermi surface and its underlying physics. A general theory has been developed to interpret the (magnetization, magnetization squared) properties of Weyl semi-metal materials, based on the semi-metal's band structure and charge carrier density. By applying this theory to TaAs, TaP, and WTe5, differences in their physical properties become evident. For example, the positive curvature of the magnetic susceptibility of TaAs is attributed to the interplay between type-A and type-B Weyl nodes, while the vanishing of the curvature of the magnetic susceptibility of TaP and WTe5 is related to the absence of type-A/B Weyl nodes and the presence of a closed Fermi surface, respectively. Notably, the magnetic susceptibility of TaP and WTe5 exhibits unusual square-law behavior under high-field static magnetization, indicating that it is possible to achieve large positive curvature of the magnetic susceptibility at low fields, which may be useful for magneto-electric applications.

Conventional differential detection can be enhanced to achieve a lower error rate when detecting continuous phase modulation signals. By modifying the conventional detector, we developed a differential detector that uses the phase information from the previous symbol to improve performance. This new detector exploits the continuous nature of CPM, resulting in a symbol error rate that can be up to 3 dB better than conventional differential detection. This error rate reduction holds true for various CPM types and data rates. The optimized detector structure consists of an inverter followed by one or two differential elements, implemented using band-pass filters. For a specific CPM format, the optimal detector performance is reached when the inverter is preceded by one differential element, which can be identified by examining the detector's frequency response. The improved performance of the new differential detector is demonstrated through simulation results, showing that it outperforms conventional differential detection by up to 2 dB in terms of symbol error rate.

To extend the validity of the molecular fluid's equation of state to higher densities, the compressibility of the system must be addressed. This involves developing an equation of state that is valid in the $\mu$-$p$ plane, where $\mu$ is the chemical potential and $p$ is the pressure. A new class of perturbative equation of state corrections has been proposed by advancing the standard virial expansion from the $\mu$-$N$ plane to the $\mu$-$p$ plane. This new expansion includes pressure-dependent two-body forces and three-body forces. The pressure-dependent two-body forces can be used to investigate the compressibility of the system, while the three-body forces serve as a measure of its validity when applying the grand canonical ensemble. A statistical mechanical approach was utilized to derive the pressure-dependent two-body forces using the anisotropic superellipsoidal potential as an example. Numerical results were obtained for the anisotropic superellipsoidal potential and they match the predicted behavior analychemically.

Recent if-then relation extraction models achieve high accuracy but rely heavily on raw text data. Our analysis reveals that these models struggle to automatically identify the hierarchy of if-then relations, even when provided for free. In fact, many models perform worse when given this additional information. By contrasting self-supervised and supervised learning as hierarchy-aware and hierarchy-ignorant knowledge, we demonstrate that models benefit significantly from relations' explicit definitions rather than their implicit presence in text. Our research shows that models can effectively learn from definitions, particularly when relations are categorized into more coarse-grained types. For example, models can distinguish between conditions that contradict each other and those that simply require additional information. They can also differentiate between promises that express potential consequences and those that represent actual effects. Our study reveals hierarchy-aware learning guidelines that enable models to prioritize learning from definitions over text data. Our results show that models trained on a combination of definitions and limited text data perform better than those trained solely on large text datasets. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various natural language processing tasks that involve conceptual hierarchies.

Our new algorithm, designed to efficiently simulate large-scale linear systems with low-rank matrices, significantly improves the performance of the HHL algorithm suited for next-generation quantum computers. This variant, which we call NISQ-HHL, provides a significant enhancement of the original HHL algorithm tailored specifically for noisy, intermediate-scale quantum machines. Our algorithm introduces key advancements, including a novel method to obtain approximate answers and a novel expansion of the inverse matrix operator with a low rank, achieving a substantial decrease of computational requirements. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of NISQ-HHL, yielding an exponential reduction of the number of quantum gates needed compared to the standard HHL algorithm. Furthermore, our algorithm facilitates approximate solutions to linear systems with matrix inverses that have a low rank, a property commonly exhibited by numerous fundamental systems encountered in applications such as linear algebra, network theory, and stochastic processes. Our findings showcase the potential of NISQ-HHL to efficiently tackle high-stakes applications like linear system sampling, important problems with implications for the security of lattice-based cryptographic protocols.

To enhance the relationship between speech representations and linguistic information, we propose the bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) to be utilized in automated speech recognition systems. BiAM's capability to direct attention both forward and backward in time enables it to effectively capture linguistic information that may be distantly embedded within a speech sequence. We have incorporated BiAM into a sequence-to-sequence transducer, and our experiments indicate a notable reduction in error rate compared to the current state-of-the-art. Specifically, we have achieved results on the Switchboard and Hub5'00 datasets with low resource conditions, yielding a 7.5% and 5.5% error rate reduction respectively when compared to the current top-performing system.

The first work to be noted is concerned with the distribution of the earliest k_n places that become available as time progresses in a dynamic parking scheme, which has been previously studied but lacks an established limits theory. To contribute to the development of a limits theory, the authors establish key results concerning the distribution of the first k_n places that become available, which they show converge to a specific distribution. Additionally, the text provides data on the speed at which the distribution of the first k_n places becomes available converges to its limiting form. It is also worth noting that the text provides an alternative proof of an result presented in the research of Aldous and Piscounov which concerns the distribution of the earliest place that becomes available.

A theoretical model has been developed to explain recent observations of superconducting nanowires, which reveal that the critical current can change in response to an applied bias voltage. By accounting for the energy band structure of the nanowire, it has been found that the effect of an applied voltage on the critical current is influenced by the type of edge states present and can be either enhanced or reduced. Numerical calculations demonstrate that the interaction between edge states and a nearby metal electrode can significantly impact the distribution of potential within the nanowire, resulting in a measurable shift in the critical voltage. It has also been discovered that the effect of an applied voltage on the critical current can be modulated by an external magnetic field, which may provide a means of controlling this effect.

Neural viewpoint-exchange networks that can generate images from novel viewpoints given text descriptions have seen significant progress recently. Our research builds upon current advancements and seeks to enhance the ability of these networks to generate videos from novel viewpoints. By leveraging a newly proposed dual representation method, our neural network is able to effectively exchange viewpoints for both static images and dynamic videos. In evaluating the dual network's ability to exchange viewpoints for novel views, we used a novel perspective corruption metric that incorporates both structural and semantic aspects. Furthermore, our system was tested on novel view synthesis from text descriptions and the results showed significant improvements compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

A crucial component in quantum communications systems is a beam splitter, and recent studies have demonstrated the possibility of creating a phase beam splitter that controls higher-order photonic modes. By contrast, developing a universal mode beam splitter that can generate specific higher-order mode phase transformations while maintaining the coherence of lower-order modes poses an significant challenge. Here, we present a design for a universal mode beam splitter that achieves the desired mode transformations by tailoring the phase and amplitude changes it induces. By employing a higher-order Laird-Smith type beam splitter with a specific parameter configuration, we show that this type of splitter can effectively maintain the coherence of lower-order modes while transforming them according to a designated pattern. In addition, we demonstrate the feasibility of realising a higher-order Laird-Smith type beam splitter using a photonic crystal waveguide with a micro-ring resonator side-coupler.

Using an expanding basis approach, we interpreted the complex resonance mass spectra of hadrons, specifically baryons, by categorizing their quantum states into different sequential patterns of energy levels. This method enables the organization of all possible quantum configurations into hierarchical structures of collective states, facilitating an understanding of the intricate resonance spectra resulting from the strong interactions between quarks. Our research revealed that the mass spectra of hadronic resonances can be explained by varying the quark-composite degrees of freedom rather than treating quarks as fundamental, elementary particles. Furthermore, we re-examined the energy level patterns of quarks and composite quarks to derive their respective potential energy curves.

To better understand the spatial spread of COVID-19, researchers need to consider aerosol transport, yet existing studies often rely on simplified models that assume aerosols are evenly distributed within a given space. To provide a more accurate representation, a team of scientists compared three different model variations - the well-mixed model, the plume model, and a combination model - by simulating the release of aerosols within a typical indoor environment. The results showed significant discrepancies between the well-mixed model and the more complex models, with the latter predicting a much higher concentration of aerosols in the immediate surrounding area but a much faster decline in aerosol concentration further away. The combination model produced similar predictions to the plume model, indicating its suitability as a simpler alternative. The study's findings suggest that even a model as basic as the plume model is essential for accurately predicting aerosol concentration and trajectory within a defined space, highlighting the limitations of the well-mixed model in capturing the detailed dynamics of aerosol spread.

Researchers examined the electrical transport properties of Cobalt and Bismuth multilayers by applying a magnetic field perpendicular to their layers. The Hall effect's scattering mechanism is influenced by Bismuth layers, where the edge-like scattering dominates up to 4 layers and the normal scattering dominates for 8 and more layers. The Hall effect's anomalous behavior stops at 8 layers and the Cobalt and Bismuth layers become indistinguishable. This phenomenon could be useful for memory devices requiring a specific resistance value. Further study is needed to understand the cobalt's oxidation effect on these layers.

In this research, we introduce a novel complex fractional quantum mechanics framework, effectively bridging the gap between the time-independent one-dimensional Schrödinger equations and their corresponding complex counterparts. By employing the Riemann-Liouville definition of fractional derivatives, we define a generalized Mittag-Leffler function and derive the complex versions of the fundamental equations. We then analyze the impact of a constant potential on the energy levels in $N$-dimensional space. Our study reveals that applying a complex potential can result in the disappearance of energy levels or their splitting into multiple levels. We also find that the real part of the complex potential primarily affects the magnitude of the energy levels, whereas their spacing remains unaffected and is determined by the fractional component $\alpha$. By further exploring a precisely solvable problem with a non-hermitian $\calP$-tunable potential, we discover that varying $\alpha$ causes a successive shift of energy levels, in addition to the ability to annihilate specific levels. Our findings suggest that the mass centre plays a crucial role in the fractionation of energy levels. Our results are in agreement with previous findings in lower dimensions and provide a higher dimensional generalization.

Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of Lipschitz regularization in constraining the activation levels of neural networks. This approach can be applied using various $p$-norms, yet the optimal choice for $p$ remains unknown. We investigated this unknown by exploring the performance of different $p$-norms in relation to a given bounded Lipschitz constant. Our findings revealed distinct regimes for $p$, each characterized by a distinct computational cost and theoretical guarantee. Specifically, we found that $p=logarithmic$ result yields the best performance, along with a theoretical guarantee of a bounded Lipschitz constant. In contrast, $p=infimum$ yield the lowest computational cost, but without any corresponding theoretical guarantee. We also established an upper bound for $p=2$, but this was found to be suboptimal compared to $p=logarithmic$. Our analysis was accompanied by empirical studies conducted on neural networks task, along with a novel approach to interpret the effect of $p$-norm. We concluded by providing guidelines for practitioners on the choice of $p$-norm in relation to different network configurations and computational resources.

The NLO$+$PS methodology, which combines fixed-order calculations for hard processes and parton showers for intermediate processes, has been effective in modeling signals for vector leptoquarks at the LHC. By integrating the differential distribution of an additional, inclusive jet, the authors of a recent study improved signal modeling and applied it to a search for $B$-physics anomalies. Using the same framework, they now conduct an optimized jet-inclusive search for the vector leptoquark $T_5$ and the scalar leptoquark $S_0$, assuming they decay into third-generation leptons. The results can be used by experimental collaborations to enhance existing searches for leptoquarks.

A novel deep learning framework has been developed to enhance the quality of low-dose PET images by utilizing simultaneously acquired MRI data. This DNN framework consists of two components: an adapter network that improves the image quality of both PET and MRI images, and a coupled neural network that enhances the PET images specifically. When applied to low-dose PET/MRI scans, the framework can significantly reduce noise. When used with conventional PET/MRI data, it can maintain image features while preserving small differences from the original images. Comparative assessments revealed that the DNN-based method outperforms conventional CT-APOD and deep learning techniques in terms of structural similarity index. Furthermore, the proposed framework has been found suitable for multi-center and large-scale applications.

Using the MSTB dataset from Chinese, this study investigates how neural coreference resolution is affected by centering theory when using contextualized embeddings. The results show that coreference resolution accuracy increases when incorporating centering theory, with the highest score achieved at 89.43%. This surpasses the current dataset benchmark. When compared to a basic neural coreference resolution model, the integrated model achieves a coreference resolution accuracy of 88.57%, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Enabling location services in WiFi-enabled devices relies on estimating the distance between the devices and reference points with known locations. These reference points, or WiFi fingerprints, are typically collected and used as geometric projections. However, accurately determining the distance between these projections and a new location point is challenging and has significant room for improvement. In fact, the distance estimates are often rough and may vary by as much as several meters in open environments. This level of inaccuracy hinders the development and deployment of various services that are vital to providing good user experiences. In response to this limitation, a machine learning-based approach has been proposed to enhance distance estimates by combining WiFi signal strength measurements with spatial information. The proposed method leverges the capabilities of graph-based neural networks to analyze probe data and location information on a map, resulting in a significant reduction in distance estimation inaccuracy to as low as 1-2 meters. The method also enables the creation of models that can be readily deployed on a variety of devices, allowing for widespread use in locations such as shopping malls, public transportation systems, and universities.

The issue of beam-induced radiofrequency breakdown limits the number of particle batches that can be accelerated in a single energy recovery linac. To overcome this constraint, researchers are exploring the concept of multi-pass energy recovery linacs to significantly boost throughput. By adopting a fill pattern that alternates between filled and empty periods in successive passes, they have found that the impact of beam-RF interactions can be minimized, thereby increasing the threshold current and allowing more batches to be processed within a single beam energy. By analyzing the interplay between beam-RF interactions, RF field decay, and fill pattern choices, experts have uncovered potential strategies to enhance performance. For example, employing a fill pattern that increases the probability of filling initially populated RF cavities can significantly delay the onset of radiofrequency breakdown, thus extending the threshold current and reducing the need to change beam energies. By optimizing fill pattern choices, researchers can enhance threshold currents by approximately 7 times, thereby greatly expanding the linac's capabilities to process multiple batches of different beam energies.

Using modern color ordering techniques, a specific component of the two-gluon correlation function was found to be non-vanishing in QCD and was expressed in terms of three-gluon and four-gluon amplitudes. It has been demonstrated that this same non-vanishing two-gluon correlation function also appears in $ \mathcal{N}=4 $ super Yang-Mills theory, in association with six-gluon amplitudes that are fully determined by dual-structure properties. By combining these results with the two-gluon correlation function, six-gluon amplitudes in $ \mathcal{N}=4 $ super Yang-Mills theory were found to be completely entangled with the two-gluon correlation function, effectively serving as "enlarged" versions of it. These findings can be viewed as an expansion of the original Bena and Draper's observation regarding the two-gluon correlation function's presence in $ \mathcal{N}=4 $ super Yang-Mills theory. In addition, six-gluon amplitudes were found to be part of a larger class of "enhanced" two-gluon correlations, with properties that lead to the cancellation of spurious poles that would otherwise contribute to sub-leading infrared terms in scattering processes.

Researchers investigated how surface curvature influences the free energy of stretching in polymer brushes near the brush-substance interface. A semi-quantum approach was used to analyze incompressible polymer brushes in the solvophilic region, yielding the brush's height and free energy when curved. When the brush is bent into a sphere of radius R, the change in free energy was found to be (3R^2*gamma_s/2R^3*R_g^2) * R^3/R_g^2 for large spheres, where gamma_s is the surface tension and R_g is the root mean square end-to-end distance of polymers. Extremely small spheres were found to have minimal surface curvature and their free energy almost equals the surface energy of the interface, but this result depends on the brush thickness. Experimental data from the incorporation of surfactants into CTAB micelles supports these findings.

A graph G is considered truncated with respect to a point set S if it contains all nodes that are a distance of D or less from S, without including any edges exceeding an distance of D from S. Our investigation focuses on determining the minimum number of reference nodes required to identify any node within a truncated version of graph G to a certain distance, and we demonstrate that this number approaches the metric dimension of G as the truncation depth increases. In particular, we can compare the Frank-Haggard bound and the number of nodes at a distance of two from a given set of references, and both distances increase with time following a specific power law. We further show that both distances can differ by a maximum of O(n) as n represents the total number of nodes in the graph.

Active galactic nuclei's long-term variability analysis is hindered by the mixed timescales involved, making it difficult to identify the underlying physical mechanisms. To tackle this challenge, a new approach called the Quasi-Dynamic Spectrum was developed to quickly extract key variability features from large datasets by circumventing the conventional periodogram analysis issues associated with long observation periods and timescale resolution limitations. This new method is particularly effective for large datasets and large dynamic spectra ranges, and it enables researchers to easily modify the algorithm parameters to balance the trade-off between feature extraction speed and timescale resolution. When put to use with simulated and real AGN light curves, the Quasi-Dynamic Spectrum proved to be a useful tool that can be refined further to meet specific research needs.

Recently, researchers have emphasized the significance of understandable and effective valuation functions in decision-making processes, particularly those involving multiple agents in complex scenarios. They have proposed two novel approaches based on bipartite matchings and directed graphs, which provide approximate representations of agents' preferences. In today's decision-making processes, often with competing priorities and limited resources, finding the optimal outcome that maximizes overall satisfaction is challenging. Utilizing the proposed valuation formats can significantly simplify this task by providing an accurate enough approximation of agent preferences. However, the quality of this approximation depends on specific conditions and scenarios. To manage this uncertainty, the researchers have established corresponding fairness guarantees based on utility, ratio, and vector maximization norms. They have also discussed various application scenarios and documented specific results for special cases. Furthermore, an intriguing connection between these fair measures and existing combinatorial optimization problems has been uncovered. Ultimately, this innovative valuation framework paves the way for a range of potential applications and may serve as a foundation for more complex valuation representations.

A practical method for detecting binary asteroids has been developed by combining image shape characteristics, specifically point spread function (PSF) features, with light curve analysis. Initially proposed techniques, such as extracting the standard deviation of surface brightness, were found to be less effective due to their limited sensitivity to small mass ratios. As a result, existing algorithms failed to accurately identify binary asteroids detected in wide-field surveys. Existing research demonstrated that binary asteroids can be identified by analyzing image shape characteristics, but it required algorithms with high mass ratio sensitivity. This, in turn, made them impractical for detecting binary asteroids found in wide-field surveys. To overcome this limitation, new techniques were developed by applying image processing algorithms to simulate the PSF of individual images and measuring the mass ratio of binary asteroids. To test these techniques, simulated images were created with various parameters, including orbital periods, mass ratios, and phase angles. The results showed that the techniques accurately detected binaries with small mass ratios. For example, one technique correctly identified 90% of mass ratios as low as 0.01. To apply these techniques to real data, mock data sets were created by simulating the constraints of wide-field surveys, including resolution limits and saturation effects. The detection effectiveness of these techniques was evaluated under realistic conditions. The research concluded that the developed techniques can be used to detect binary asteroids found in wide-field surveys, with the most effective being the application of light curve parameters to images, followed by the use of image shape analysis techniques, specifically

To gauge the significance of network influences in economic research, economists often rely on methods that analyze connections and node relationships in networks. Existing approaches mainly focus on accounting for peer effects or quantify their impact, yet fail to provide precise measurements necessary for policy interventions. To address this limitation, researchers have developed innovative techniques to estimate network peer effects, leveraging topological network data and outcome measurements. In a recent study, authors Jin-Andrew Chen, Yuliy Rosser, and Hui Yu developed a framework to extract relevant peer effects from complex networks and applied it to analysis of social influences within online communities. Utilizing tools from topological network analysis, regression techniques, and metric embedding, their method involves utility maximization through the revelation of underlying peer structures. When testing their approach on simulated data and evaluating it against alternatives, results show that their method offers superior performance and accuracy. Furthermore, the authors successfully demonstrate their approach's practical applications by examining information diffusion, identity formation, and competition for influence within Reddit forums.

This study develops multiple chain rule formulas for the variable-order fractional operator, creating different expressions that can be viewed or contrasted with existing methods. We derive various forms of the chain rule in relation to Riemann-Liouville, Caputo, and Mittag-Leffler operators, and explore their connections. We also examine the cases where the order belongs to specific intervals, and establish relationships between the different forms. Our results contribute to the understanding of these operators and their applications in solving fractional differential equations.

To evaluate the effectiveness of different agents' interaction methods in a collaborative game, we developed a test environment based on the 'Treasure Hunt' scenario. The game features two competing teams and incorporates elements of chance, goal-seeking, and theory of mind. We tested four agents' interaction approaches in this environment: random, rule-based, state-based, and theory-of-mind driven. Our experiments investigated how the incorporation of a theory-of-mind approach affects goal achievement, puzzle solving speed, and knowledge sharing among agents. The results showed that the theory-of-mind approach is the most effective method in achieving goals and solving puzzles, although it may delay the initial goal achievement. Furthermore, agents using the theory-of-mind approach often share false knowledge, indicating a need for future work on refining this approach.

Our analysis reveals that a specific protein, known as PDB 4ZOH, possesses a shallow knot and employs an uncommon folding mechanism compared to knotted proteins it is grouped with. Contrary to the conventional theory that knotted proteins fold via a similar pathway as their non-knotted counterparts, this study discovered that 4ZOH's unique topology prevents it from utilizing the same folding route as other knotted proteins. Instead, it follows a distinct pathway more similar to those used by its non-knotted peers, likely indicating that folding mechanisms are more diverse and subject to change than previously believed.

Given a symplectic form $\omega$ on a symplectic manifold $M$, an irrationality condition can be imposed such that a subset $B$ of positive integers doesn't share a common factor with the integers resulting from a specific mapping of homology classes. It has been proven that this irrationality property can be equivalently defined in terms of a certain full measure subset of $B$ that has a specified pairwise relatively prime property. This subset can be used to demonstrate the existence of a unique topological property - in the case of a symplectic mapping torus $T_\omega \mathbb{Z}$ - namely, $T_\omega \mathbb{Z}$ has a distinct algebraic topology defined by the image of the mapping torus map, in addition to its defined symplectic structure. Additionally, this implies that any symplectic mapping torus $T_\omega \mathbb{Z}$ with a specific property has a unique topological property, thereby providing an evidence for the Tomanov-Vust Timpani conjecture in a specific case.

A theoretical model involving kaon condensation is used to explain how a type of massive Nambu-Goldstone boson can obtain its mass. This involves a non-vanishing quantum expectation value of a field combination that is connected to the symmetry-breaking parameter and is analogous to what occurs in the Higgs mechanism. This leads to an equation that resembles the one derived through the effective field theory of chiral perturbation theory, but with an additional constraint that can result in a mass value that may exceed the intrinsic mass limit by itself. This can occur even when the condensation scale exceeds the intrinsic mass scale, even if it doesn't generally happen due to the approximate symmetry breaking in QCD. This prediction can potentially be verified through experiments using heavy ion collisions that may lead to a type of matter where the kaon condensation could generate a mass value that might be detectable, given that it could occur at a density level that might be achievable with certain types of heavy ion beams.

Our research introduces DISCO, a novel counterfactual data generation framework that
provides a straightforward method for enhancing machine learning model performance.
By utilizing influential counterfactual examples that can impact classification decisions,
our approach creates synthetic data that significantly improves model robustness and
generalization when training on limited datasets. Our findings show that employing
DISCO-trained models leads to superior results compared to standard data generation
techniques, with notable improvements when working with scarce data. Specifically,
our results indicate a notable 48% enhancement in model robustness when employing
counterfactual data with only 5% of the original dataset.

Researchers who grow materials on graphene substrates have found that it's possible to create epitaxial domains through a process called surface reconstruction, but the process's outcomes are heavily influenced by the growth temperature and it's challenging to predict the material's final structure as a result. In a breakthrough study, a method has been developed to grow hexagonal domains of boron nitride on a graphene layer at an elevated temperature, only to discover that lowering the growth temperature causes it to transform into octagonal and square domains of boron nitride. By using hexagonal domains as a template, researchers were also able to grow hexagonal domains of graphene that surround them and isolate them from larger hexagonal domains of graphene. As a result of this unique structure, researchers have observed the emergence of a hexagonal domain of a ferroelectric material called hafnium oxide that has never been seen before.

We establish new rank bounds for codes possessing a $ \Z_3 \Z_9$-linear structure, effectively surpassing previous records by a significant margin. These codes, incorporating elements from the finite field $\F_{3^6}$, are encoded using a $ \Z_3 \Z_9$-additive architecture with a specific parameterization, thereby enabling the creation of a vast class of linear codes with specific properties, including Griesmer bounds for codes of dimension $2k$ and rank $k$. Moreover, our findings reveal that our $ \Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes can translate into $ \Z_9$-additive codes, thereby establishing new records for the former and tying previous records for the latter, with both having a rank of $k=3$ and achieving the Griesmer bound.

Working with multi-label classification problems often necessitates substantial dataset annotations, presenting a significant barrier for many applications.  To address this challenge, we developed a method called single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling, which generates valuable multi-label data with minimal costs by leveraging existing single-label resources.  When utilizing these samples to train classification models, we observed improvements of up to 12% in classification accuracy.  We also compared our approach to alternative sampling methods by conducting extensive experiments across multiple task and dataset combinations, demonstrating its effectiveness.  The code and datasets used in our experiments are now publicly available.

We define 'weakly natural transformations' between functors and reveal they don't require the usual naturality condition for establishing a universal property related to adjunctions. Our results demonstrate that the property of being a weak natural transformation makes up a category where the 2-category of functors, often considered in categorical contexts, factors through a subcategory of 2-categorical functors. This finding leads to a revised understanding of the concept of natural transformations and the categories they define. Additionally, we discover a connection between weak natural transformations and the hom-functor, notably finding that the property of being a weak natural transformation can be expressed using the hom-functor and identities.

To understand the behavior of blazars and their gamma-ray emissions, accurate modeling of the radiation processes within the jet is crucial. By comparing different models, we found that the radiation process involving electron pairs, known as the two-component electron model or the 'Pair-Accretion Disk' (PAD) model, effectively explains high-energy observations but has a limitation when addressing the spectral peak above 1 GeV. By incorporating a radiation-reversed self-consistent pair production process, the PAD model becomes robust, capable of predicting a wide range of spectra, including those peaks that exceed 1 GeV. By utilizing this PAD model in a comprehensive simulation of 45 prominent blazars, we found that it accurately accounts for gamma-ray data across a wide energy spectrum, regardless of the spectral peak. Furthermore, this PAD model, in conjunction with imaging, provides a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of blazars, giving rise to possible connections with their gamma-ray spectra.

Deep neural networks have effectively detected cardiac abnormalities by outsourcing intelligence to complex models, but these models are prone to dataset overfitting and struggle with noisy data, thereby limiting their applicability in real-world settings.  A novel, lightweight detection framework is presented, utilizing a linear residual operator to combine feature representations for both robust excitation and stabilization of internal parameters, thereby preventing overfitting and ensuring generalization across diverse datasets, including those with significant noise levels.  Experimental evaluations, conducted on datasets for detecting cardiac abnormalities, heart valve abnormalities, and lung nodules, demonstrate the proposed method's capability to achieve superior performance, reducing overfitting 20-fold or more, and significantly improves model detectability, accuracy, and consistency, by 25% or more, by 10% or more, and 15% or more, respectively.  Code availability at: https://github.com/zhongjiao-li/LRO.

Mobile health applications have encountered data privacy challenges due to strict confidentiality requirements in medical data.  Wearable activity recognition has the potential to contribute to breakthroughs in various fields such as insulin dosage recommendation and exercise intensity measurement.  To address the issue of privacy, researchers have developed a method to maintain confidentiality by keeping health data encrypted.  However, this has created a barrier to improving accuracy through collaborative learning.  A new protocol called FedHealth has been developed which enhances the accuracy of wearable activity recognition by 21.8% and 15.8% in comparison to traditional methods, while keeping the data confidential.  A team of researchers compared FedHealth with other protocols and found that it achieved better results in a real-world trial among 30 participants.  Furthermore, FedHealth was found to reduce the amount of data exchanged between devices and servers by 7.9% and 5.7%.  A team of experts also found that FedHealth enhanced the security of wearable activity recognition by 25.6% and 20.9%. Portfolio management across multiple time frames and organizations involves making strategic decisions that balance competing objectives, including risk and reward, and optimizes decision-making processes. The complexity of these decisions calls for optimized solutions that can effectively handle uncertain data and varying priorities. This study explores the application of optimization techniques in portfolio management, delving into the theoretical underpinnings and real-world implementations of utility-based and multi-objective optimization methods for portfolio selection and management. The study's primary contribution lies in its classification of optimization approaches on a conceptual and practical plane, which serves as a foundation for evaluating existing research and potential areas for future work. Furthermore, the study's findings have implications for the development of risk management frameworks and optimization algorithms.

The recruitment process involves creating panels for interviews and scheduling them, 
which can be time-consuming and require significant resources. To address this challenge, 
this paper presents an algorithmic framework that leverages the strengths of two techniques, 
dynamic programming and graph theory, to efficiently manage the process. For large-scale 
applications, the framework utilizes a cloud-based environment to achieve optimal results. 
To validate the effectiveness of this approach, the paper includes results from a mock 
recruitment process at a higher education institution in Australia. Compared to conventional 
methods, the proposed approach yields superior outcomes in terms of efficiency and productivity.

We are examining the case where a underlying diffusion is present and its impact is being studied on the value of a forward-start option. This type of option is paying off the greater value between the difference between two stocks at two future time points, for a specific number of stocks and with the ability to choose variables that affect its payoff. Our analysis involves creating a new method to solve a type of stochastic differential equation that takes into account both past and future information. This equation includes two components: one that solves a backward stochastic differential equation with a given function as its final value, and another that solves a forward stochastic differential equation with a given function as its current value. Our new method involves developing a type of change of measure called the change of measure of Girsanov, as well as establishing its uniqueness. Our results also involve creating an optimal payoff that maximizes expected value, as well as comparing it to the forward-start option.

To explain the anomalous magnetic moment of the neutrino, we propose an asymmetric leptoquark production process at future electron-positron colliders, such as the ILC or FCC. By doing so, we investigate the capability of this process to surpass the limitations of top quark production and provide a potential new way to detect top quarks at these facilities. We establish minimum requirements for leptoquarks to be detectable as we consider various combinations of leptoquark flavors and charges that could give rise to top quark signals. We then compare the asymptotic efficiency of leptoquark production through the usual pair production method and the asymmetric method. Additionally, we examine the capability of the ILC or FCC to detect leptoquarks with masses beyond their respective maximum capabilities.

We investigated a distinctive feature in extreme starburst galaxies that shows high abundance of heavy element ions in their outflows and gas reservoirs, using a simplified two-phase model. By analyzing a sample of 24 galaxies with high energy spectroscopy data, we found a correlation between the formation of heavy element ions and the energy emitted, as well as variations in ion abundance that could be explained by changes in gas density. A comparison with theoretical predictions from a two-phase model revealed that a low-density phase, influencing the abundance of certain ions, might exist in the gas reservoirs surrounding these galaxies. Furthermore, an analysis of the absorption lines in the spectra revealed that the physics of the gas remains consistent across different observational distances from the galaxies.

Consider a Cayley graph based on the Hamming distance for a finite group G, defined as the set of permutations of a d-symbol vector to its nearest neighbors. Let's denote this graph as Γ_G(d) and examine its subgraph consisting of reachable states from a central state Δ under the Hamming distance, up to a distance th d from the center. Now imagine overlaying two copies of this same subgraph, one with the set of metric balls Δ_ε and the other Ω_δ, both centered on Δ. Our goal is to identify the largest intersection of these two subgraphs, generalizing a previous idea by Alspore and Gorodezky to find the minimum number of steps to reach a specific state while adhering to certain protocols. We can rewrite this problem to find the minimum number of steps to leave the intersection region while applying the error Δ_ε and the alteration Ω_δ. We have developed a formula to determine the largest intersection of two metric balls in Γ_G(d) for low errors and a specific distance, calculating the minimum number of steps required to leave this intersection.

The detection of Gravitational Waves from Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs) relies heavily on accurate models of pulsar timing. Closed-form analytic expressions for the fractional frequency drift, influenced by General Relativity, have been developed but approximate certain small terms. I compared these expressions with two alternative methods: (1) a numerical solver for the pulsar's orbital parameters and (2) semi-analytical techniques. The accuracy of the approximate expressions was evaluated for individual pulsars and combined datasets from two PTA experiments. While the approximate expressions accurately match the semi-analytical method, they were found to be less precise than the numerical solver, with differences of up to $6.5 \times 10^{-20}$ Hz/s when considering individual pulsars. However, when using the numerical solver to compare the semi-analytical and approximate methods against the true values, the differences were found to be very small, at a level of $1.2 \times 10^{-21}$ Hz/s for individual pulsars and $0.5 \times 10^{-21}$ Hz/s when considering combined datasets. Consequently, the approximate expressions are considered suitable for use in PTA experiments.

We have demonstrated that in ASEP, the velocity distribution of a distinguished particle with different speed, whose initial position has a specific probability distribution, evolves in a specific way over time. Our findings show that the probability of it moving at a particular speed at time t is given by a determinantal formula, which arises from applying the time-evolved natural interface operator to a specific set of discrete monic polynomial functions. As a result, we gain explicit expressions for expectations of various symbolic functions, which correspond to expectations of the number of steps the particle travels, the number of sites it visits, and the order of its nearest neighbors. Moreover, we are able to derive moments of these symbolic functions, facilitating the investigation of asymptotic behavior as the system becomes infinite. Additionally, we establish convergence of these moments to solutions of a non-linear integro-differential equation, which describes the time-evolved velocity of a second-class particle in ASEP. Furthermore, we examine the limit of an infinite system to determine the asymptotic velocity of the particle, a notion that is otherwise poorly understood.

When modeling epidemiological systems, researchers often fit differential equation models to available data to make predictions and understand complex dynamics. However, it's crucial to ensure that the proposed model aligns with biological constraints to prevent fitting artifacts from overshadowing essential analytical insights. In this paper, we introduce a Bayesian approach that fits multi-component systems modeled by differential equations, taking into account feasibility conditions that reflect real-world limitations and assumptions. We apply this approach to a model of antibiotic resistance, incorporating feasibility constraints that reflect realistic population dynamics. By combining the model fit with the biological interpretation, we can distinguish true phenomena from those caused by data fitting. Our method allows us to assess the impact of different data sets on the model's validity and provides a way to weigh different model components based on available data.

In a recent finding applicable to ultracold atoms and molecules, a combination of standard pendulum theory and Rayleigh-Pitman law called the effective non-rigid pendulum model has been developed to demonstrate its usefulness in a specific scenario. By adopting a specific unitary transformation, the non-rigid pendulum model was shown to mimic the behavior of a quantum system where atom-molecule conversions occur, and it reveals that the Fock state dynamics have analogous features to the non-rigid pendulum's classical dynamics. Furthermore, the model reveals that the Fock state's stability boundary coincides with the classical pendulum's non-rigid variant, and it indicates that the breakdown of integrability occurs at the same nonegative integer ratio of $1.5$, both having the same root cause of over-tuning. The model's validity has been verified through comparisons with both the original quantum system and the classical non-rigid pendulum, and it provides exact expressions for system-specific effective parameters that could be beneficial for experimental manipulation.

As DNA data storage gains popularity, effective management of storage partitions becomes essential to support large-scale applications. In a DNA data storage system, retrieving encoded data relies on precise sequence information, but this information is subject to change over time. A critical issue arises from the limited ability to maintain up-to-date reading templates, known as primer pairs, which are essential for decoding. To address this challenge, our proposed approach develops an automatic design framework for primer pairs that can adapt to changes in the stored data and efficiently handle large-scale applications. By leveraging a linear programming problem to minimize storage space while maintaining readability, our framework offers multiple benefits, including reduced storage requirements, improved resilience against sequence errors, and streamlined reading operations. To facilitate real-world implementation, our approach is coupled with an integer linear programming problem to manage storage partitions for repeated sequence segments. Comprehensive simulations validate our approach, revealing improved performance compared to existing methods.

This research introduces the Principal Component Geostatistical Approach (PCGA), an enhanced sparse Bayesian learning method that leverages prior information to accurately model riverbed bathymetry from flow velocity measurements. By applying PCGA to a challenging problem where the number of observations exceeds the grid size, we significantly improve upon existing methods in multiple aspects. Our results show that PCGA yields superior performance in estimating riverbed bathymetry, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods in multiple metrics. Our approach also enables efficient state estimation by incorporating prior information in the sparse representation, resulting in a direct solution to the inverse problem. Furthermore, PCGA is capable of handling large models with ease, resulting in exact solutions in scenarios where other methods may produce suboptimal results due to model size limitations. Our code for PCGA is publicly available on GitHub, and we demonstrate the method's effectiveness on synthetic data and real-world data from the Mississippi River.

Our research introduces an innovative approach to creating High Dynamic Range (HDR) images by leveraging a dataset with singly exposed images. Our method surpasses existing techniques by utilizing a dataset with automatically set exposure settings. Our approach consists of two primary components: an Enhanced Tone Mapping Network (ETMN) and a Quality-aware Quality-aware Exposure Estimation Network (QEEN). The ETMN produces an HDR image from a singly exposed image and an initially estimated exposure map. This map is then refined by QEEN, which takes the difference between the original and the initially estimated HDR images. Our method achieves improved results according to the HDR-VDP-2 metric and the weighted score of the HDR image quality metric.

Identifying research gaps in the field of causal deep learning has become increasingly challenging due to its rapid growth. A new framework is proposed to organize existing methods and guide future research by categorizing techniques into four areas: relationship induction, data set construction, model assessment, and model improvement. By viewing the field through these four lenses, researchers can pinpoint opportunities for future work and potential solutions to existing problems. A causal deep learning landscape is presented, featuring notable research gaps in areas like model assessment and ways in which future research can build upon existing methods in model improvement. A preliminary outline is also provided for a causal deep learning cookbook that could facilitate collaboration within the field.

This note provides an updated proof of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, effectively linking the result to 20 years of topological advancements, specifically the interconnection of the B-principle, the b-stable theorem, and 3-dimensional manifold classification.

This research develops an aggregate two-level BDDC preconditioner for symmetric, positive definite, and linearly algebraic systems derived from general finite element methods. The performance of a linearized version of the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) algorithm is examined through various experiments. Key factors influencing the algorithm's effectiveness, including the degree of polynomial used for basis functions and subdomain partitioning designs, are investigated. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed two-level BDDC preconditioner produces excellent convergence rates for a wide range of problems and problem sizes. Furthermore, the research highlights important guidelines for selecting suitable coarse and local smoothing levels, as well as strategies for adjusting the degree of polynomial basis functions to achieve optimal results, with the (elastic) Saint Venant's problem serving as a representative test case.

An interesting phenomenon observed in the brain's neural systems and certain types of financial networks has sparked investigation into a specific class of random processes - alpha-stable diffusion processes. However, the challenge lies in reversing the direction of time to accurately infer these processes from partially reversed data. This issue is particularly pronounced when attempting to reverse the direction of time for alpha-stable processes defined on a continuous domain. A recent breakthrough enabled the time-reversal of discrete alpha-stable processes, yet the corresponding algorithms require an unreasonably large sample size to function effectively. This study aims to circumvent this limitation by developing a new time-reversal algorithm tailored for continuous alpha-stable processes. This approach leverages a Gaussian-based approximation, takes into account the variances of the processes, and assumes a specific type of directional flow. Furthermore, the accuracy of this algorithm is demonstrated through numerical experiments conducted on realistic models of correlated and heterogeneous systems.

Researchers who use nonlinear optics often study loop resonators due to their ability to generate identical counterpropagating light modes with different phase relationships, thereby allowing the investigation of nonlinear effects such as cross-phase and self-phase modulation. A theoretical model is now an extension of previous work, enabling the comparison of cross-phase and self-phase modulation in a loop resonator with identical counterpropagating modes. It was discovered that cross-phase modulation exhibits a stronger tendency to cause mode locking than self-phase modulation, although self-phase modulation is generally more prominent. A unique feature of loop resonators is the ability to swap the relative phases of the counterpropagating modes, which can completely switch the effectiveness of cross-phase and self-phase modulation. A loop resonator's ability to maintain identity of the counterpropagating modes also allows for the nonreciprocity of nonlinear effects to be studied, which could be beneficial for the development of magnetic-free nonreciprocal devices.

A novel multiscale super-resolution GAN model has been developed to improve the resolution of turbulent flow simulations across multiple scales. To evaluate the model's effectiveness, it was applied to three different simulations of turbulent channel flow with different Reynolds numbers, resulting in a high-resolution simulation of flow phenomena such as vortex layers and streamwise-aligned cobblestones. By comparing the model's results to original low-resolution simulations, increased $R_e$ simulations showed a 50% reduction in momentum drag and a 25% increase in streamwise velocity. Additionally, the model demonstrated improved prediction capabilities for high-resolution vortices above 200 km-1 and skin friction coefficients above 20 km-1.

We present a new evaluation method that utilizes controlled variations in progressive curriculum design to assess the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms. In typical assessment procedures, a single optimized curriculum is used to evaluate an reinforcement learning method for an extended period. However, we propose incorporating a curriculum optimization cost into the evaluation of these methods. This is because learning agents benefit significantly if they can adapt their own curricula in response to performance improvements. We leverage progressive curriculum learning as a framework and investigate key aspects. Firstly, we reveal how altering the curriculum structure affects the performance of these methods and highlights their individual characteristics. Moreover, we propose utilizing a controlled metric to evaluate the robustness of these methods and incorporate this metric into the evaluation protocol. Finally, we propose combining the curriculum optimization cost with the standard performance metrics as the final evaluation score. We demonstrate the applicability and usefulness of this method by conducting experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets.

Process mining techniques have advanced significantly, enabling the analysis of evolving business processes. Previous research introduced an approach to comparing process models, which identified differences in process logic. Another development, known as DCR graphs, delves into discovering variations in process behavior over time. These DCR graphs distinguish dynamic aspects of processes and pinpoint changes in process patterns. In real-world settings, processes interact with their environment, influencing future process development. With this interplay in mind, we propose an enhanced DCR framework highlighting the reciprocal relationship between process changes and their environmental impacts. This framework's potential is demonstrated through a case study exploring the evolution of a process related to invoice handling, uncovering subtle interactions affecting the process's future development.

Notions of compactifications for moduli spaces of algebraic varieties are explored through both geometric and Hodge-theoretic approaches. It is shown that while these methods yield equivalent outcomes for certain types of varieties, known as hyper-Kahler manifolds, they result in distinct compactifications for others. This distinction holds, even in the case of varieties with specific properties, known as generalized Kähler-Einstein fluids, for which the geometric and Hodge-theoretic compactifications are non-birational. Furthermore, non-basical conjugate pairs of varieties can be identified, providing which the geometric compactification is not special, whereas the Hodge-theoretic one is. It is also demonstrated that varieties lacking a particular property, which we call "geometric good reduction," can be compactified through a specific geometric approach, resulting in a compactification with an integral model. This finding is particularly significant as it enables the utilization of analytical tools for such varieties.

An examination of a large sample of galaxies from the GALEX and Sloan Digital Sky Survey reveals an unexpected pattern where galaxies with greater mass than 10 to the power of 10.5 solar masses exhibit positively correlated colors in the near ultraviolet spectrum. This observed color correlation contradicts the conventional view that the rest frame ultraviolet colors of galaxies decline as they increase in mass. A deeper look into a subset of galaxies with available optical data reveals that the observed color pattern holds true and provides evidence for a transition in galaxy behavior at masses greater than 10 to the power of 10.5 solar masses. This finding stands in opposition to previous research and may signal a more profound shift in galaxy characteristics that requires further investigation.

Knowledge distillation has been effective in improving performance on a target task by using knowledge from a more competent but hard-to-use pre-trained neural transfer model. Most approaches, however, limit the application to within the same language. We investigate cross-language knowledge distillation and find that it can significantly enhance the performance of a resource-constrained model when trained to express a specific sentiment in a language different from the original one. The key challenge arises from the lack of parallel data, which can be addressed by using existing multilingual pre-trained models as teachers. We propose a novel soft labeling method that takes into account the direction of interest and utilizes multiple teachers to increase efficiency. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms traditional training methods and other baselines across four different language pairs, achieving an average gain of 5.5% in sentiment classification accuracy.

An analysis of patient data who required intensive care due to COVID-19 reveals significant variations in treatment requirements and health outcomes. To enhance the effectiveness of limited healthcare resources, we propose an approach that evaluates specific features associated with a patient's ICU admission. These features, which are derived from statistical summaries of ICU admissions, enable healthcare providers to prioritize patients based on their predicted treatment needs and likely recovery trajectories. By applying machine learning to these features, we can accurately identify patients who require high-intensity treatment and allocate scarce resources more efficiently. Furthermore, our approach facilitates an equitable distribution of resources by giving priority to patients who are more likely to benefit from intensive treatment. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by conducting numerical experiments on real data collected from Australian ICU admissions.

The connection between the universal bundle functor and the simplicical group monad is characterized by an explicit natural transformation. This characterization enables the extension of this relationship to the category of simplicial groups with arbitrary parameters, providing a definition of the universal bundle functor as it relates to simplicial group structures. Our main contribution involves proposing Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), a new data augmentation technique that enhances the efficiency of VRD modeling by reducing the need for negative proposal sampling. Compared to standard negative proposal sampling, BNPS yields VRD model accuracy improvements of 4.5% and 2.5% using the VenqueVision9K and Vision90 datasets respectively. Our approach achieves these gains without increasing the number of positive proposals sampled. BNPS works by dividing negative proposals into three categories and selectively sampling from them. Our results show that limiting negative proposal sampling to only inductive proposals results in a 1.5% accuracy decrease, whereas sampling random proposals and induction proposals yields the best accuracy. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates robustness to different sampling ratios and allows for a 10 times reduction in sampled proposals while maintaining accuracy levels.

The galactic bulge is thought to originate from the merger of multiple small galaxies, but accurate simulation of this process is hindered by the lack of a clear understanding of how galaxies interact and merge. We developed a new method to simulate galaxy interactions using a high-resolution, hybrid smooth-hydro smooth-particle hydrodynamics approach and applied it to an extensive set of accretion scenarios, including both isolated and cosmologically competitive environments. By post-processing the simulation data, we generated high-definition images of galaxies at different stages of interaction and merger. These images demonstrate how galaxy interactions influence their structural development and morphology. In isolated systems, we found that the accretion of a small galaxy can delay the formation of a bulge, while massive mergers result in the formation of massive bulges. In contrast, multiple smaller mergers may lead to the creation of peanut-shaped bulges. In competing cosmological environments, we found that the probability of multiple smaller mergers increases with time, ultimately leading to the formation of a peanut-shaped bulge, and the accretion of a large galaxy can result in the formation of massive stars and a prolonged bulge formation period.

A profoundly intense solar flare along with widespread coronal mass ejections occurred on November 7th, 2004.  The event was strong enough to cause noticeable disturbances in interplanetary space and allowed researchers to utilize data from multiple sources to conduct a comprehensive analysis.  By examining data from various instruments including solar extreme ultraviolet, X-ray, and UV observations, researchers uncovered the detailed characteristics of the flare and surrounding energetic particle events.  Furthermore, data from Earth-bound detectors at low and high altitudes allowed for an in-depth look at the effects of the solar activity on the upper and lower atmospheres.

This research investigated KIC 9267654, a solar-type star exhibiting unusual light fluctuations and rapid spin, and sought possible explanations for its distinct characteristics. By analyzing data from the Kepler space telescope, we discovered an irregular rotation pattern and identified oscillation modes that could aid in understanding the star's internal composition and rotation history. We used two methods to study the star's rotation and core properties and found its core to be less dense than expected, with a possible explanation being a partial merger scenario with a low-mass companion that slowed core rotation. Another possibility is that the star interacted with a low-mass companion that caused mass transfer, resulting in an expanded core and variable rotation patterns.

Fake news has been a growing concern on social media, and detecting it requires advanced techniques due to the abundance of misleading information.  To tackle this challenge, an innovative approach called MetaFEND is proposed, consisting of a multi-layer detection framework that addresses the diversity of fake news.  This framework includes multiple task-aware detectors, a common feature extractor, and a tiered detection process.  To train the model, a data preparation method called selective sampling is developed, leveraging social media platforms' built-in reporting mechanisms.  The effectiveness of MetaFEND is demonstrated through benchmark experiments on the FEVER dataset, yielding superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.  The code and model for MetaFEND are available at https://github.com/ghafoul/MetaFEND.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional transport equation featuring nonlocal flux and periodic conditions, without dissipation effects. The study investigates solutions to the equation and reveals that they shed light on a specific shock formation criterion. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate that a particular type of solution exhibits a singular growth rate, in line with a previously established result by the second author. The research also explores solutions to a related nonlocal Burgers equation and nonlocal KdV equation. The associated project involves creating and contributing code for the nonlocal KdV equation to the open-source project ODE-solver, as well as developing a nonlocal solver utility.

This research reveals that a quaternary Golay array pair QCAGA of order 2n x 2n can be created if a quaternary Golay array of order n x n exists, along with a binary Golay array pair BAGA of order 2n x 2n and a binary Golay array of order n x n.
