We establish a fundamental basis for the quantum group U_q(g) labeled by the set of positive roots of g, and confirm that it fits within the framework defined by Lusztig's beta-map, exhibiting properties including invariance under the braid group action and Dynkin automorphisms.

A recent cryptocurrency-based scheme known as Forsage has used a decentralized approach to recruit users and process payments, using a hierarchical structure that allows transactions to be processed quickly and efficiently. By analyzing Forsage's user data and transaction history, researchers were able to gain insight into the project's underlying structure and the financial motivations of its users. The data reveals that nearly all Forsage users participate in a pyramid scheme and experience financial losses. In fact, the researchers found that only about 0.2% of users do not experience losses. The Forsage project's decentralized approach and use of smart contracts may have helped reduce transaction fees, attract more users, and increase the speed at which transactions are processed. The success of Forsage also seems to have created a model that other similar projects are trying to emulate by mimicking its code and structure. The Forsage project has been operational since mid-2019 and has paid out millions of dollars to its users. The researchers suggest that the project's popularity can be attributed to its ability to offer high returns to early investors and its decentralized and automated approach to processing transactions. The Forsage project's hierarchy has grown rapidly, with a large number of users participating in the scheme, including some high-stakes participants who are willing to invest large amounts of money in the project. The researchers also found evidence of users who are trying to manipulate the project's structure and code to their advantage, as well as users who are trying to identify Forsage's administrators and gain an advantage

Two new globular cluster candidates have been discovered in the Milky Way's third density plateau using data from the VVV survey, and three previously suspected clusters were verified as globular clusters. The newly found candidates, located near the globular cluster Ter 2, are both highly distorted and Ter 2's neighboring small alpha globular cluster are likely the result of a gravitational interaction that occurred around 100-300 million years ago. The current analysis is based on high-precision colour-temperature measurements from a extensive catalog of highly probable variable stars within the VVV survey. By comparing the observed colour-magnitude diagrams against theoretical isochrones, it was determined that the three confirmed clusters have an age range of approximately 9-11 billion years and are located at a distance of about 6,500 light years from Earth. Additionally, an extensive comparison was made with existing catalog entries to contribute new data on the already known properties and variables associated with Ter 2 and its surrounding clusters.

We present a novel class of erasure correction codes, utilizing a specific type of tensor network that can be visualized as a graph with loops. This class includes the GHZ diamond construct, the Werner states, and the Husimi-Quntum states as specific examples. A tensor network of this type can be considered a code if it meets the following requirements: the action of the erasure channel on its distilled form results in a null state, and the retention of its original form when some symbols are erased. If the tensor network consists of a single type of tensor, we show that its ability to correct erasures is equivalent to satisfying a specific condition related to its eigenvalues, and that this condition must result in a completely anti-symmetric structure when trying to correct $n$-qubit erasures using a $d$-dimensional tensor network. If the tensor network consists of different types of tensors, we show that its ability to correct erasures is equivalent to satisfying a defined set of matrix equations, and that this network can correctly erase a $n$-qubit system if it has a loopy graph structure that is completely connected. If the tensor network consists of a single type of tensor acting as a code for the erasure of up to $d-1$ qubits, we show that its ability to correct erasures is equivalent to satisfying a defined set of conditions related to its eigenvalues, and that this network can correctly erase a $n$-qubit system

Understanding how a business process evolves over time is crucial for creating effective, data-driven decisions. To achieve this, it's essential to analyze the relationships between process stages and the associated predictions. Our proposed framework enables users to capture complex relationships between process stages by utilizing graph neural networks, and our results show this approach outperforms traditional methods by achieving a 10% improvement in performance. Furthermore, our methodology allows for timely predictions by accounting for process stage evolution, and our findings indicate a significant 25% enhancement in predictive power when considering temporal factors.

Let $\Phi$ be a smooth function that satisfies certain conditions and defines the Gelfand-Shilov space $H^{s,p}(\mathbb{R}^n).$ We establish estimates for a broad class of functions $f,$ characterized by their behavior under differentiation and convolution, and show they are equivalent to growth conditions for their Fourier transforms. These results yield detailed characterizations of the spaces $H^{s,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and related spaces, and we also investigate their connection to pseudodifferential operators.

We performed an in-depth analysis of a rare and exceptionally bright 2010 June 7 solar flare that exhibited significant and prolonged variations in multiple wavelength ranges. Our primary focus was on examining the behavior of hydrogen lines and the impact of the flare's magnetic field. We gathered high-resolution spectra from the Solar Optical Spectrograph at the National Solar Observatory's Global Solar Telescop and complementary data from the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory's UltraViolet Spectral Energy Distribution instrument. We analyzed the time it took for the Ly-alpha line to return to its pre-flare state, finding it to be approximately 5.5 days. Furthermore, we observed significant line broadening in hydrogen lines, particularly in the UV range, which we attribute to the presence of a magnetic field. This interpretation is supported by comparisons with synthetic spectra generated using the PHOENIX code. We also studied the temporal evolution of the optical and far-ultraviolet continuum, noting its pre-peak onset, which we speculate could be related to the activation of radiative acceleration of electrons. Additionally, we calculated the total energy emitted in the hydrogen continuum and estimated it to be roughly 1.5 times that emitted in the continuum bands we examined.

Our primary contribution involves developing a novel TPC framework that achieves a significant enhancement in the certified accuracy of point cloud models against twisting transformations, resulting in improved performance. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed TPC architecture by achieving enhanced results in the adverse transfer learning setting, thereby increasing the robustness of point cloud models. Our proposed method achieves notable gains in both general and adaptive certified accuracy across multiple twisting transformations. Our approach also obtains superior results in adverse transfer learning, surpassing the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin.

The RPA approach is employed to investigate the poles associated with the electric dipole giant resonance of oxygen-16. By applying a complex scaling transformation to the RPA equations, the RPA poles are studied as the scaling parameter varies. A detailed analysis of the initially scalar states reveals two distinct poles that correspond to the (1-) and (3-1) states of the electric dipole giant resonance. Furthermore, the momentum distributions of these states provide valuable information about their resonance characteristics. Additionally, a perturbative approach is used to enhance the accuracy of results by incorporating higher-order corrections. The findings agree with previous studies utilizing the RPA alone. The complex scaling method offers significant benefits in momentum space, allowing for easier evaluation of form factors compared to configuration space. The resulting momentum-dependent energy levels and form factors exhibit unique properties that arise from the interplay between the RPA poles and the complex scaling transformation.

A recent analysis of certain nonlinear systems using the Koopman operator theory has been compellingly shown to be equivalent to a network analysis. Researchers have been able to reconstruct the underlying dynamics by shifting their focus from the nonlinear equations to the operator form and subsequently extracting valuable insights from the resulting smooth equations. This approach has been found to provide a clear picture of the system's structure and has facilitated detection of its instability through the calculation of spectral properties. Our proposed method presents a way to study a nonlinear system defined by multiple equations, whose dynamic relationships are interconnected in a complex network format. By applying the Koopman operator theory to each individual component and combining the resulting smooth equations, we have developed a way to explore the system's global dynamics, as well as its underlying architecture, by linking the operator's properties to its network format and announcing a result that enables the detection of its stability and network format conditions.

Our research introduces Sparse Generative Adversarial Networks, a novel GAN-based model capable of limited-word sentence generation. Unlike current sequence GANs that rank word importance, our SparseGAN model assigns a dense set of importance values, one for each word in each sentence. By taking the maximum of these values, we obtain a sparse sentence representation that can be used for various tasks and significantly accelerates training by restricting word selection to already learned patterns. By leveraging a dense importance vector, our model achieves superior results in various sparse text generation tasks such as Chinese and English news summaries, outperforming the current state-of-the-art approaches by significant margins of 12.3% and 23.8% respectively in compression ratios.

The task of detecting life beyond Earth faces a significant challenge due to the limited observational capabilities for studying extraterrestrial biosignatures in gas. However, the surface of asteroids and comets may provide a more feasible alternative by offering a direct pathway to investigating interstellar panspermia. By analyzing the current limitations and constraints for detecting life on celestial bodies associated with small body missions, we propose a new focus on identifying environments that could support microbial life and, by extension, may indicate the presence of interstellar seeds. A future mission could then prioritize the analysis of these environments for biomarkers in both terrestrial and extraterrestrial settings. Given the existing small body mission techniques, we suggest a novel approach for a future mission that could utilize existing capabilities to optimize the detection of biosignatures in asteroids and comets by combining multiple analyses of varying priorities. By applying this flexible approach, a mission could potentially identify microbial life or evidence of panspermia on celestial bodies like Ceres, Enceladus, and Saturn's outer moons by examining their surface composition, geology, and associated environments for signs of life.

Animal population density research often relies on release-recapture methods, but these can be time-consuming and costly, or provide incomplete data, making it difficult to pinpoint subjects and gather essential location information. Recent advances in capture-recapture methods using partial data have led to two-dimensional density estimates, but these are typically assumed to represent uniform distributions, neglecting the benefits of Bayesian methods that can account for specified movement patterns. We present a Bayesian approach to modeling the movement of animals subject to partial data capture, using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods to simulate random movements and density maps, and applying these to a study of polar bear movement. These methods can be valuable tools for researchers studying the movements and populations of free-ranging animals.

A crucial aspect of multilayer networks that contains diverse interactions and relationships between multiple groups requires a heightened sense of stability analysis. Conducting a thorough examination of the network's stability through its linearized dynamics can be extremely computationally intensive. A recently proposed simplified approach can potentially analyze the network's stability by converting it into an equivalent single-layer network, yet this method has limitations when applied to multilayer systems with distinct interaction layers. We have now expanded this approach to accommodate such complex networks by treating each distinct interaction layer as a separate node within a single-equation system. This enhanced method enables a streamlined analysis of the network's stability by applying various techniques such as the eigenvalue decomposition of a single-equation matrix or the calculation of a single-equation matrix's spectral radius. We have tested this expanded approach on a variety of multilayer systems, including a recent power grid scenario, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness.

Let's consider two modules, D and M, defined over a differential ring R. An operator Delta is established to map from the set of derivations on R to the set of twisted derivatives associated with M, while another operator Gamma is defined to map from the set of twisted derivatives associated with M to the set of derivatives associated with D, with the property that Gamma is parametrized by Delta. In other words, Gamma and Delta form a parametric relationship, where Gamma is parameterized by Delta. With this relationship in mind, we aim to explore and analyze the conditions under which Gamma is parameterized by Delta, ultimately leading to the classification of parametric relationships between operators Delta and Gamma.

Our novel, fully automated testing system for detecting and fixing programming mistakes builds upon our previous proof-of-concept, expanding its capabilities to accommodate a wide range of programming languages and incorporating sophisticated techniques that enhance efficiency. By utilizing sophisticated graph-matching algorithms, the system compares expected against actual program behavior, identifying points of inaccuracy and prescribing fixes. Developed using standard testing frameworks, the system's effectiveness was demonstrated through tests written in Java, Python, and C, resulting in a 97% success rate in detecting and resolving errors on a diverse set of real-world test cases.

The paper investigates the Phillips-Sarig theory, focusing on root systems of types A and D. A key concept in the theory is the relationship between a root and its reflection, which forms a pair. The paper reveals an interesting phenomenon where all pairs share the same "height." This result stems from the fact that the maximal root in these root systems exceeds all others in terms of height. The paper also explores connections between its findings and certain algebraic structures known as braid groups and fundamental representations. Additionally, it establishes relationships between root system pairs and the associated Coxeter groups.

In a typical distributed setting, the algorithmic problem of interest may be too complex to solve at a individual node, prompting the need for a decentralized approach. This paper addresses such challenges in network environments. We develop a randomized distributed algorithm for estimating a network's size in an unknown graph, applicable to various network types, including general information-rich networks. The proposed method requires only two rounds of node communications and yields an accurate size estimate with a single message exchange in the final round. The accuracy of the estimate can be adjusted to trade off precision for a smaller message size. The algorithm's versatility allows it to accommodate multiple network scenarios, including those with node degree limitations. A theoretical analysis of the algorithm's performance provides guaranteed upper bounds on its computational and memory consumption. To facilitate practical implementation, we also outline a sample protocol for executing the algorithm on standard multi-hop wireless networks.

Recent nonparametric approaches to estimating queue lengths based on observed waiting times have shown promise, outperforming traditional parametric methods in terms of accuracy. In contrast to parametric methods that require specific distribution assumptions, these nonparametric methods provide general solutions applicable to various queue configurations. Specifically, the research presented utilizes perspective-taking to interpret waiting time data, resulting in accurate queue length estimates. Furthermore, the studies conducted demonstrate the superiority of nonparametric methods over parametric ones in terms of accuracy, with improvements observed in the order of 20-30%. The findings discussed have implications for the design of systems and services vulnerable to queueing phenomena.

We've developed a novel approach to resolving the Hamiltonian constraint, allowing for a higher degree of freedom in the choice of conformal factors while maintaining stability and accuracy. This method creates a separate grid for solving the constraint and employs linearised updates to achieve a second-order convergence rate, surpassing the limitations of conventional conformal normal gauge methods. Our scheme's distinctive feature is its ability to utilize multiple, freely chosen conformal factors, effectively bypassing the issues associated with the conformal factor itself. Our results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques, including spectral conformal methods, by achieving a 30 times higher convergence rate with comparable computational costs. Furthermore, our scheme successfully applies to both flat and curved spacetime scenarios.

Anomalous thermal transport phenomena in solid materials have been largely unexplored.  This work predicts unique thermal transport properties in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites RCrO3 (where R stands for rare earth elements) by utilizing a theoretical framework that incorporates their intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement.  Anomalous Nernst effect and anomalous thermal conductivity differences from the common thermal transport trends are found in these materials.  Rare earth element variations influence the magnetic configuration, leading to changes in thermal transport, and could potentially result in experimental manifestations.  Experimental verification of these predictions is feasible due to the materials' integration in functional oxide films.

User facilities like synchrotron light sources and electron microscopes serve as key drivers of innovation in materials research, enabling researchers to develop new methods and experimental techniques that in turn drive material discovery and advancement. By leveraging these facilities to explore materials and their properties at multiple length and time scales, scientists have made significant discoveries that have propelled the development of new techniques. In order to enhance the impact of these facilities, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology is working to integrate its own user facilities with local research capabilities in order to foster a collaborative environment that sparks new research and opens up opportunities for technological advancement. By taking a holistic approach that combines user facilities, simulation capabilities, and research expertise, HKUST is positioning itself as a leader in the development of materials and nano-technologies.

We establish new results concerning the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, given data that varies over time and space. Under specific conditions on the obstacle's initial configuration and a surrounding environment, we prove that a particular solution satisfies a specific PDE and meets certain boundary conditions. Our investigation into the Sobolev regularity of this solution reveals that the gradient of the solution belongs to a specific class that allows for the application of an improved regularity criterion, resulting in a higher level of Sobolev regularity for the solution's gradient near areas where the obstacle is not defined. Our approach to achieving these results involves utilizing techniques such as time-average and space-time averages of the obstacle's initial configuration, as well as the application of an improved version of an earlier regularity criterion.

Hangyung Chiu investigates certain Galois coycles, which the community has started to explore, albeit briefly, in previous discussions. His work delves into the analysis of these coycles in the context of reductions modulo p of crystalline extensions. Specifically, he examines reduced crystalline extensions and finds they are equivalent to purely ramified extensions or combinations of fully split and wildly ramified extensions, depending on specific p-values. Furthermore, he uncovers conditions under which two such extensions are isomorphic and identifies a specific subset of his found coycles that correlate to global Galois coycles. These findings deepen the understanding of G_K-Artin-Scheier coycles and their connection to reductions of crystalline extensions.

We have established that in a specific higher-dimensional space, a hypersurface whose mean curvature is bounded can be composed of multiple regions, each defined by distinct hyperplane equations, arranged in layers with specific parabolic shapes. This result provides a new framework for understanding certain aspects of randomly generated hypersurfaces and generalizes an earlier one-dimensional theory to multiple dimensions. As an additional contribution, we apply this theory to better comprehend the characteristics of hypersurfaces that arise from randomly moving boundary surfaces in certain higher-dimensional stochastic models.

This research introduces a novel self-sensing concrete composite that utilizes carbon nanotubes to detect damage through electrical resistance changes. By leveraging the consistent relationship between resistance variations and mechanical strain, a genetic algorithm can effectively enhance the accuracy of damage identification by comparing simulated resistance data with real-time measurements from the composite. A numerical model is utilized to generate resistance changes resulting from mechanical loading, and these are compared with actual measurements to refine the model's accuracy. By integrating the genetic algorithm with the nanotube composite's self-sensing capability, damage can be reliably detected, thereby enabling the effective utilization of this technology in safety-critical applications.

We have developed a generalized Lotka-Volterra model that incorporates complex predator-prey interactions into a dynamical system with four dimensions. This system allows us to explore various scenarios of a three-species system with one intelligent species that can adapt to its environment. We have discovered distinct outcomes, including the coexistence of all three species, the extinction of the two non-intelligent species with the intelligent species surviving, or the intelligent species becoming extinct with the two non-intelligent species competing for a common resource. Additionally, this system exhibits all possible combinations of these outcomes when we consider both the species that can adapt and the species that cannot as either predators or prey.

We define a new type of mathematical object, which we call a 'combination', that comprises a collection of geometric vectors along a curve in n-dimensional space. We demonstrate how these combinations can be used to prove several important identities related to integral geometry. These identities were previously established but our proof provides a distinct approach using analytic methods. Additionally, our approach reveals relationships between these identities and certain integral inequalities. These inequalities, in turn, are equivalent to well-known geometric inequalities such as the Brunn-Minkowski inequality, the Alexandrov-Fenchel inequality, and the Reeds-Shephard inequality. Our method also offers a novel geometric interpretation of polar transformation and a new approach to solving reverse Holder inequalities.

We propose an explanation for the observed discrepancy in the muon magnetic anomaly by postulating the existence of an additional light gauge field that interacts with the muon and eludes detection. To verify this theory, future experiments with a beam dump or a mobile neutrino detector will be necessary to explore a significant portion of the relevant parameter space by several orders of magnitude. In our suggested scenario, the future J-PARK muon experiment at the J-PARK facility, utilizing a 4.5 GeV storage ring, will be able to significantly encompass the entire accessible spectrum of parameters. In our proposed setup, we calculate the predicted signatures, such as specific neutrino channels that should be monitored, and estimated event rates that could indicate the presence of this new physics. In our discussion, we also consider alternative explanations, such as a dark parity preserving $U(1)_A$ force, and outline the distinct signatures that would indicate these theories are correct.

A comprehensive analysis of spin-three Ward identities for the $sl(2)$ symmetric Toda conformal field theories reveals a deeper connection to higher-spin symmetry. By integrating the spin-3 currents and a single Toda field with respect to their respective charges, we derive a set of charge-neutral spin-three operators whose collective symmetry gives rise to higher-spin symmetry. A key aspect is that these neutral operators cannot be expressed in terms of primary fields alone and require the inclusion of descendent fields in their definition. A distinction arises between the $A_{n+1}$ and $B_{n+1}$ series Toda field theories, determined by their respective level parameters and associated conformal spectra. A previous observation linking the Toda coset construction with the semi-symmetric Neveu-Schwarz sector is further elucidated by the emergence of a doublet of neutral operators, whose collective symmetry represents the full NS$_{s}$ higher-spin algebra. A derivation of the spin-three Ward identities from a coset construction perspective rounds out the understanding of higher-spin symmetry within the Toda conformal field theories.

A geometrically finite lattice in a hyperbolic space of any dimension is consistently automatic, thereby proving that it is bi-automatic. This result can also be applied to consistently automatic lattices in hyperbolic spaces of dimensions two, three, and four, as these depend on specific properties and are bi-automatic under certain conditions.

Previous research suggests that brain-machine interface technology using high-resolution cortical recordings can accurately predict walking capabilities in individuals with spinal cord injuries. To facilitate seamless, natural interaction with such a system, it's essential to compare the precision of cortical recordings in determining gait functions. In a study involving 10 participants with chronic, severe spinal cord injuries, we used high-density electrocortical recordings while they walked on a treadmill. Our machine learning model successfully predicted key gait parameters including stride length, stride speed, and swallowing frequency during walking. Comparison with a more conventional EEG approach revealed an average 2.5-fold improvement in precision. We further enhanced the precision by integrating a differential decoder and a state-estimation method, a technique known as filter-learn. This approach resulted in a 3.5-fold increase in accuracy when compared to standard EEG. Our findings demonstrate the superiority of cortical recordings over traditional EEG in predicting complex gait functions and suggest that precise prediction of movement capabilities requires a system that distinguishes artefacts from meaningful signals.

Let $\mathbb{A}$ be a right-angled Artin group associated with a graph $\Gamma$, acting on a tree $\mathbb{T}$ with axes that are geodesics.  A subgraph $\Delta$ of $\Gamma$ is defined as **separating** if there exist vertices $v$ and $w$ in $\mathbb{T}$ such that the group generated by the edge stabilizers in $\mathbb{A}$ corresponding to $\Delta$ acts transitively on the edge segment between $v$ and $w$ in $\mathbb{T}$, yet it does not act transitively on any proper segment containing $v$ or $w$.  We prove that a subgraph $\Delta$ of $\Gamma$ is separating if and only if the subgroup corresponding to $\Delta$ has index 2 in the subgroup generated by edge stabilizers containing a given element of the group $\mathbb{A}$, and this result enables us to characterize the subgraphs of $\Gamma$ that are not separating.

Dynamic graph neural networks often rely on node degree updates to capture evolving graph topologies, but this approach can lead to degree explosion and slow learning due to undirected edges. Contrary to this common practice, our proposed DECENNT model deliberately keeps undirected edges constant, effectively creating a decentralized network from a nearby assignment, and leverages these fixed connections to accelerate learning on temporal data. We demonstrate the benefits of decentralized networks through DECENNT's improved performance on time-evolving graphs, both on large-scale dataset submissions and complex graph-based benchmark tests.

The observation of individual particles or entire populations of biological agents such as bacteria, cells, proteins or RNA is a fundamental aspect in fields like biomedical and environmental research, yet accurately differentiating their movement from that of non-biological objects like fluids or solids is crucial. A novel image processing method is presented that combines active contour models with optical flow algorithms to analyze two-dimensional time-lapse images, allowing for the correction of particle trajectories affected by confounding hydrodynamic effects, sedimentation or temperature changes.

In optimization theory, the Nested Neumann algorithm has been demonstrated to achieve fast linear convergence near optimal solutions by leveraging the inception depth property. A recent study extended the algorithm's applicability to exhibit the inception property's in-depth implications on the underlying problem structure. Here, we investigate a variant of the nested algorithm and show that it can be applied to optimize a class of convex functions defined on a tree-like graph, thus highlighting the property's versatility. Furthermore, we provide a new property, the ``child-parent'' condition, which serves as a prerequisite for both the inception depth and the Nested Neumann algorithm. This condition enables us to develop a new algorithm and establish its linear convergence rate. Our research is complemented by an example from the field of convex geometry.

Identifying the topological characteristics of Anderson insulators in complex systems appears challenging due to the destructive nature of measurements that fluorescence signals must necessarily employ. A team of researchers suggests utilizing defects or impurities as "quantum meters" to measure these properties by analyzing their interactions with the surrounding environment. In their model, defects coupled to multiple modes will yield a specific outcome when the topological structure exhibits a particular "handedness," which serves as the basis for detecting this handedness. This approach enables the detection of the topological structure by measuring the properties of the defects, separating their individual contributions from the environment. Moreover, the researchers demonstrate how this method can be applied to vision-like systems, such as atomic arrays and photonic lattices, to detect the handedness of their surrounding environment. As a further application, they show that the method can be used to investigate the topological structure of vision-like systems that are coupled to their environment, as well as the behavior of atomic arrays and photonic lattices in Anderson's monopole regime.

Research indicates that genus-one curves possess unique, independently defined geometric characteristics that remain unchanged, unaffected by various computational approaches. Our study utilizes the explicit formula for generating functions of invariants to demonstrate the distinct nature of these characteristics. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that defining relationships between the geometric properties and endosomal invariants hold true for genus-one curves, thereby confirming previous observations made by physicists.

To understand how the production of heavy Higgs bosons, resulting from an extended electroweak symmetry breaking theory, is affected by the phases of the complex parameters and the properties of squarks, we need to examine the interactions between squarks and the heavy Higgs bosons. We calculated the contributions of squark effects to the production of the heavy CP-even Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and found his cross-section to be significant, reaching up to 80 nb for certain collider operating conditions and assuming certain ranges for the squark and gluino masses. Furthermore, we observed that the phase of the complex parameter $\mu$ affects the squark decay modes and thus influences the final states of the heavy Higgs boson productions, while the phases of the complex parameters also impact the cross-sections of the heavy CP-odd and the lighter CP-even Higgs bosons.

In contextual linear bandits, selecting optimal actions requires significant communication costs.  A recent approach uses context-based linear value function estimates to accelerate decision-making.  We analyze two key aspects:  first, we establish lower and upper bounds on the context distribution's knowledge impact on communication costs;  second, we investigate two contexts: one where an agent can freely choose contexts and another standard fixed context setting.  In the former, we find that the upper bound on effective dimension is increased by 1; in the latter, we find the minimum achievable effective dimension is 1.  We also develop two new policies for contextual linear bandits and compare their performance against existing methods.

This paper explores the potential benefits of policy learning algorithms that produce highly efficient value function estimates when working with large datasets. Unlike conventional approaches that minimize the impact of sample size in value function estimation, our research reveals that larger test sample sizes can significantly improve the performance of value function estimates and subsequently the policy learning outcome. To take advantage of this finding, we develop a new policy learning framework that balances data utilization between value function estimation and policy evaluation. Within this framework, we establish theoretical bounds on value function error and sample size requirements to ensure policy optimality. Our results are further illustrated through synthetic data examples and real-world crowdsourcing applications.

Our research examined the transverse momentum distributions of charged hadrons, pions, kaons, and protons in various collision systems, and found their relationships to elliptic flow patterns. We identified similar trends in pion and charged hadron distributions, and observed distinct patterns between kaon and proton distributions. By studying these patterns and incorporating particle identification data, we aimed to gain insight into the role of radial flow in particle production. We also developed a statistical model to compare our findings with existing data and theories. Our results are significant because we investigated the correlations between radial flow, elliptic flow, and particle spectra, and provided new guidelines for future studies.

Our research examines two simple binary and continuous power control schemes in large-scale wireless networks with many transmitters and receivers. We found that in these networks, the schemes can effectively manage strong interference. Binary power control, for example, can silence overwhelmed receivers, while continuous power control can limit the power transmitted to overwhelmed receivers. We compared these schemes to the optimal approach, which aims to maximize data transfer in these networks. We developed algorithms to determine if the binary and continuous power control schemes perform as well as the optimal approach. In networks with multiple frequency channels, we found that the binary power control scheme performs similarly to the optimal approach, whereas in networks with limited frequency channels, the scheme performs significantly worse. In contrast, the continuous power control scheme performs similarly to the optimal approach in both types of networks.

We introduce a multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA) for numerically solving general time-dependent partial differential equations, specifically designed to handle equations with distinct slow and fast timescales in particle-laden flows. By splitting equations into sub-systems governed by these timescales, we employ different solvers to solve each sub-system, significantly enhancing computational efficiency. A key feature of MTSA is its ability to use high-order schemes for sub-systems with rapid timescales, while employing conditional stability-preserving methods for the primary system. We demonstrate the advantages of our algorithm by applying it to two scenarios: a single particle in a shear flow, and a complex scenario with multiple particles interacting in a flow. Comparative studies show that MTSA yields comparable results to traditional methods while achieving substantial computational savings, with the greatest benefits obtained in multi-scale simulations.

It is possible to express $7^n$ as a sum of two positive integers $a$ and $b$, where it holds that $a-b = 1$ and $a$ is divisible by $b$. This expression leads to a sequence of congruences, ultimately resulting in the modular relationship $7^{2n+1} \equiv 2 \pmod{3n+1}$, with $n$ being any non-negative integer.

A key challenge in robotic hopping arises from the lack of precise information about ground contact, necessitating the development of a control strategy that enables a robot to track desired trajectories even with uncertain ground contact conditions. This study presents a feedback control approach for a robotic hopper with a spring-like leg system, building on the concept of an augmented state variable that includes robotic hinge positions and velocities. By applying this control method, we were able to demonstrate effective trajectory tracking capabilities for the robotic hopper across a range of ground contact scenarios, even with no prior knowledge required about the ground. In fact, as the augmented state variable feedback control approach relies solely on measurement data, it can be implemented using standard feedback control protocols commonly found in commercial motion controllers. In our experiments, the robotic hopper successfully tracked predetermined trajectories with precision, achieving tracking errors of less than 10 centimeters within a 1.5 meter tracking distance.

To calculate the difference in radius squared for various meson states made of quarks and antiquarks, we used a linear combination of correlators of two current operators in a hot medium. We calculated the expected values of these differences using the hard thermal loop perturbation theory, taking into account the temperature effects and calculating the radius differences as order-to-order contributions to a series. Our results for the differences in radius squared for mesons made of identical quark flavors are presented as a series valid for small masses, with the first few order-to-order contributions explicitly given.

We introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model, a probabilistic framework that combines a topic model and hierarchical directory models to facilitate the analysis of information networks. Based on the MCMC algorithm, we derive the expected value of hierarchical topics and documents to develop an efficient sampling method. We apply the proposed method to networks represented by text and derive the posterior distribution of topics within each document. Additionally, we leverage the algorithm to enhance existing text analysis techniques by incorporating the hierarchical structure of networks. Experimental results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing LDA-based technique in terms of both diversity and density of obtained topics. Furthermore, we demonstrate the proposed algorithm's capability to enhance the existing LDA-based technique by incorporating the hierarchical network structure, leading to more precise retrieval of focused topics.

Quantum annealing has found applications in complex optimization and sampling across various fields, albeit with limited practical implementation thus far. The success of quantum annealing relies on its ability to navigate the "annealing gap" - a range where classical computational power is hindered, yet the algorithm still requires decision-making. pinpointing the annealing gap's boundary is crucial for developing quantum annealing protocols and identifying suitable problems to solve. Our research developed two key metrics to characterize the annealing gap's duration and width, utilizing the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) in combination with classical computational resources. By optimizing QAOA's depth and employing a novel "threshold crossover" technique, we significantly increased the gap, achieving results up to 35 times better than the standard QAOA. Our findings were validated across multiple random graph problems and the Shimony-Hein-Verstraete entanglement generation scenario. The strategies we developed are compatible with the Quantum Ascii Processor Unit (QAPU) and could be adapted for other quantum annealers.

This research focuses on theoretical modeling to predict the electronic band structures and material properties of several nickelates, using a combination of accurate crystallographic data and advanced computational methods. By applying state-of-the-art relaxation and symmetry-breaking corrections, we accurately reconstructed the band structures of MeNBO (n = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) for their respective ground states. Our findings reveal that the unique band shapes, resulting from strong covalency effects, dictate the materials' magnetic and superconducting properties. We further used a simplified phase diagram to investigate possible ground states and predicted that the recently discovered superconductor GdNCl with electron filling x = 4.5 might exhibit dual ground states and fascinating physical properties.

The structure of quark stars is examined in a dense medium model, using a modified MIT bag model that incorporates a deconfinement phase transition, to investigate how this transition affects the stars' characteristics. Comparing the medium model to the standard MIT bag model reveals a key difference: the former yields equations of state that change sign at a critical density, whereas the latter produces equations of state that always increase with density. As a result, the presence of a deconfinement phase transition in the medium model results in a change in the equation of state's behavior at a certain high density, with implications for the mass and radius of quark stars. Additionally, we find that the causality condition restricts the radius of quark stars to be less than 15 kilometers, and that the presence of the phase transition can influence the mass-range limit of quark stars, causing it to increase by as much as 0.75 solar masses in the medium model.

One of the compass's key functions is to determine orientation. Yet, another fundamental capability, closely tied to this function, is measuring environmental parameters that affect directionality, such as thermal noise affecting damping rates. We examine the interplay between two key aspects in the compass's ability to measure these parameters and its ability to determine orientation. Initially, we analyze how the compass's state variance affects its ability to estimate the damping parameter. Our findings indicate that the precision of this estimation decreases exponentially as the state variance increases. We then investigate the effects of variance on the compass's ability to determine orientation and find that this ability becomes impaired once the state variance surpasses a certain threshold. We also explore different control methods, assess the compass's thermal evolution, and examine the interplay between the number of measurement data, state variance, and orientation determination. We demonstrate that high variance can hinder orientation determination and that certain control strategies can mitigate this effect. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the compass's thermal evolution, variance, and orientation determination.

Evaluating the development of protoplanetary disk cooling is crucial for understanding planet formation and how it affects the surrounding environment. To effectively solve the radiative heat transfer equation, researchers typically employ Monte Carlo methods or Monte Carlo-Taylor expansions due to the complex nature of gas and dust interactions, resulting in a full radiative transfer solution. Nonetheless, a straightforward analytical approximation exists, which can be utilized for post-processed analysis or as a prototype for more intricate solutions. This approximation prioritizes an in-depth analysis of the cooling efficiency in the outer disk regions, facilitated by a dust grain temperature model. As a key finding, it was discovered that dust particles exert a significant influence on cooling efficiency in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Consequently, a precise determination of disk cooling patterns depends heavily on the employed dust grain radius. Furthermore, comparing previous studies that overestimated the cooling efficiency by several factors reveals the potential risks of misinterpreting observed disk characteristics. Additionally, the potential biases in estimated mass accretion rates are also discussed.

This research focuses on obtaining estimates for harmonic functions within specific growth rates, relating to a particular class of geometric structures known as gradient shrinking Ricci solitons. It demonstrates that a harmonic function $f$ satisfies the bound $f(x)\leq A\left(1+\sup_{B(x,2r)}f\right)/r^{\alpha}$ for a constant $\alpha$ greater than 0, for a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton satisfying a growth condition of order $\omega(r^{-\epsilon})$ with a small enough positive value of $\epsilon$, and assumes a minimum point distance of $d_0$ and a minimum harmonic function value of $f_0$, provided that the point $x$ lies within a certain distant point $d(x, D(x,r)) > d_0$ and a maximum value $\sup_{B(x,2r)}f$ is defined. It also shows that a bounded harmonic function must be constant under the same conditions.

Dynamic backdoor attacks involve manipulating models to misinterpret specific data patterns as malicious labels. These attacks can be complicated to execute, however, as they require training a separate model or inserting fake data into the large dataset used for model training. Such limitations make these attacks impractical for real-world applications where large datasets are typically used to train models. In response to these challenges, this paper proposes a novel dynamic backdoor attack called Token Noise, which injects artificial features into the data used to train models, features that model a function determined by the malicious pattern it is designed to target. Unlike conventional methods, this attack does not necessitate training a separate model or inserting fake data into large datasets and can effectively create a dynamic backdoor in models. Furthermore, this attack's effectiveness is demonstrated across multiple classification tasks by applying it to models trained on smaller datasets and evaluating its impact, following best practices for reproducibility and rigorous testing.

By using high-precision astrometric data from the Gaia satellite to locate the positions of two specific stellar streams, we discovered that the technique of gravitational lensing can be employed to detect a minute shift in parallax, along the path of these streams. A detailed analysis revealed the shift to be influenced by both ecliptic latitude and a specific pattern of alignment with the line connecting the Sun and the center of the galaxy. By combining a lensing algorithm with Monte Carlo simulations, we found that the technique can not only detect streams with a certain brightness but also reveal previously concealed streams, particularly those with a specific orientation relative to the solar system. A future space telescope with an order of magnitude greater precision, similar to a advanced version of Gaia, is expected to be capable of detecting the lensing effect on individual stars within the Scorpius-Centaurus association, a young nearby star cluster.

Using a semantic approach, our knowledge graph-based model incorporates knowledge in Q&A systems by enhancing relevance rather than exact matching. Unlike traditional methods that rely on exact matching between knowledge and input, our approach leverages graph similarity to combine knowledge and neural Q&A techniques. This resulted in a novel framework where knowledge is incorporated into the model through an attention mechanism, leading to a significant improvement in Q&A performance compared to baseline methods that utilize extensive knowledge. Our approach also enables neural Q&A models to effectively utilize vast amounts of discrete knowledge without requiring extensive training data, as confirmed by our scaled experiment.

Determining the structures of negatively charged molecules is increasingly difficult, especially for small compounds containing oxygen, whose spectral data often reveal multiple possible combinations of bonds, rendering it challenging to pinpoint their exact shapes. In the absence of clear experimental evidence, theoretical predictions based on possible arrangements of electrons and nuclei can vary greatly, making it crucial to develop comprehensive theoretical models that can match a wide range of experimental techniques. Nevertheless, creating such all-encompassing models can be complicated due to the need to balance the level of detail and accuracy, in addition to accommodating a broad spectrum of experimental data, including both valence and core-electron information. The latter can be particularly challenging, as it necessitates incorporating high-energy spectroscopies, such as X-ray spectroscopies, that can reveal details about core electrons and their interactions with valence electrons. The development of our BSSD theoretical approach across a wide range of charged oxygen-containing molecules, from small to large, is demonstrated herein. This approach leverages a combination of theoretical calculations and experimental data to produce detailed, all-encompassing models that can match both valence and core-electron information. As a result, we have created a comprehensive set of theoretical predictions for 43 ions, along with corresponding experimental data, available for download and further analysis.
