A novel approach to analyzing rotating stars under the influence of gravity is presented, where a new method of property assignment is used that differs from conventional techniques. This technique involves directly solving the Eulerian-Polar fluid equation system, written in a conserved form, and uses a conservative assignment of mass, angular momentum, and thermal energy to fluid elements. A non-uniform grid is employed to increase the accuracy of calculations when comparing to the uniform grid method. This research also develops an iterative method to determine property assignment values at each grid point, and includes numerical boundary conditions to maintain physical and mathematical integrity. Multiple test cases are ran to validate the proposed method, and it outperforms the uniform grid technique in nearly every aspect.

Acquiring comprehensive labeled data is a significant challenge that limits the widespread effectiveness of machine learning. This issue is compounded in contexts where data collection costs scale linearly with the amount of data, a common occurrence in many real-world situations. Our research presents a novel approach to addressing this problem by developing an active learning framework that leverages an inexpensive method to label a subset of data, representing either features or classes, which can then be combined with an unsupervised representation to train a machine learning model. Our approach generates results across multiple datasets and scenarios, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, our active learning framework provides data labeling recommendations that minimize costs and efficiently utilize limited label resources.

The observation of neutron stars after their merger through high-energy electromagnetic radiation has so far been observed in fewer events than detected emitting gravitational waves. To better understand these merger events, a future enhanced electromagnetic monitor in the sky will be necessary to comprehensively study sources in various directions. In the current era, I analyze the most notable neutron star merger events detected through both gravitational and electromagnetic waves. I then consider the existing observational capabilities and potential future telescopes to calculate the detection rates of neutron stars after their merger at different high-energy frequencies. By doing so, I determine the optimal locations in the sky to focus electromagnetic monitors on, in order to facilitate a deeper understanding of these events.

This research examines the impact of the pandemic on diversity of urban encounters and community resilience in Toronto. By analyzing aggregated data of over 1 million encounters in high-density public spaces, we found a significant decline in diversity of encounters during the pandemic period lasting over a year. This decline resulted in increased inequality among community members as only a limited number of socially privileged groups continued frequenting these spaces. As a consequence, we observed a shift in diversity of encounters from being primarily socioeconomic in nature to being mainly defined by income and occupation during the pandemic. Furthermore, our study revealed notable differences in community resilience in different neighborhoods with those having higher diversity of encounters and a more inclusive community exhibiting greater resilience.

Around a young and massive (approximately 20 solar masses) star called G9'1, researchers discovered a disk surrounding a void left by a massive protostar and observed matter moving along predetermined paths as it migrated towards the star. To understand these findings, a mathematical model was developed to analyze the effects of objects moving within the disk's outer region on its inner portion. Contrary to expectations, it was discovered that particles moving countercurrent to their normal course could create a stable zone around the star and that those moving in circular paths could significantly impact the star's temperature. Furthermore, data revealed that the inner disk's dynamics changed over time as objects moved and interacted with each other, influencing the distribution of matter and altering the environment in which they moved.

This research paper introduces an innovative method to enhance the Eulerian formulation of water wave problems by utilizing a technique called the Method of Fundamentals. By applying this method, the surface elevation and velocity potential are expressed in terms of a small number of fundamental functions, enabling efficient reconstruction of high-amplitude waves. Damping terms are also naturally incorporated into the system. When only considering deep water and finite surfaces, the approach enables explicit time-domain calculations. Furthermore, the relationship between the wave envelope and surface elevation can be accurately established, allowing for surface elevation reconstruction through the inverse method. A numerical example highlighting the advantage of this approach over existing Eulerian methods is presented.

We provide a detailed examination of the surface layer theorem in locally convex spaces. This involves demonstrating the convergence of a sequence of differential forms, which lie within a compact subset of a given space, and have vanishing integrals over that subset. Our findings build upon previous work by the second author and others, and result in an application to the analysis of a sample theorem related to differential forms.

This paper introduces a novel layered control structure for a mobile robot equipped with sonar sensors.  The layered control system takes proximity information to navigate an known environment.  A top-level controller uses a grid-based representation to guide the robot, while a bottom-level controller utilizes a local metric space for navigation.  The system's design takes advantage of both the precise proximity data from the sonar sensors and the existing environmental map.  As a result, the layered control system offers improved robustness and the ability to operate in dynamic environments.  The proposed approach has been tested and demonstrated to be effective, as evidenced by the data presented from real-world experiments conducted in a variety of settings.

Neural News Digest is a text summarization system that uses complex documents. It consists of a dataset with 1,000 items, structured into three levels: it includes a large dataset with 900 items, a small dataset with 20 items for model selection, and a tiny dataset with 1 item for final model selection. It employs a hierarchical multi-task learning model to facilitate the exchange of information between related tasks. It incorporates a context-aware fake news detection model that utilizes a dataset with 1,000 items to distinguish genuine and fabricated news. It utilizes a hierarchical attention mechanism to differentiate relevant and contextual information. It enables the model to differentiate essential and non-essential information. It employs a complex loss function that incorporates multiple information sources. It results in a significant enhancement in performance when utilizing vast amounts of contextual information. It surpasses the baseline model by an average of 10% accuracy. It achieves accuracy rates of 67%, 72%, and 77% in the small, medium, and large datasets, respectively. It obtains an f1-score of 67%, 72%, and 77% in the same datasets. It obtains a 45% precision rate and a 73% recall rate in the tiny dataset. It obtains a precision rate of 45% and a recall rate of 73% in the small, medium, and large datasets. It achieves a 73% precision rate and a 45% recall rate in the tiny dataset.

Researchers commonly employ the curvature effect as a significant factor that can steer system behavior but have historically viewed it as a fixed property. This study reveals that treating the curvature as dynamic may yield a more in-depth understanding of various phenomena and reveals its intricate relationship with system entropy and hysteresis, presenting a novel perspective that may be applied to studying nonlinear interactions. A key finding shows that the curvature itself adapts dynamically in response to the system's interactions and the surrounding environment, influencing whether the system exhibits hysteresis or not. By viewing the curvature as a variable, a new dynamic equation can be formulated, revealing that the curvature's change rate is directly proportional to the system's entropy, thus providing a possible explanation for the origin of hysteresis. This novel perspective also enables the development of an information entropy metric that can be used to evaluate the complexity of nonlinear interactions and is tested using real data from an experimental study of a nonlinear mechanical system exhibiting hysteresis, showing that it aligns with previous findings and presents a promising future direction for studying nonlinear interactions and hysteresis.

We address the challenging problem of L1-Principal Component Analysis (L1-PCA) when data is embedded in a high-dimensional space with D^N points, yet assumes rotational invariance. A two-block formulation is proposed, where we factor the original problem into two independent problems: one extracting sparse, rotationally invariant signals, and the other constructing orthogonal transformation matrices. This two-step approach enables the development of an approximation solution using random orthogonal matrices, leading to the scaled L1-PCA (SL1-PCA) method. A global measure of solution accuracy is established and proven to decrease with increasing data size. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this two-step approach, as well as the importance of generating true rather than arbitrary rotation matrices.

Our proposed framework combines quality control and semantic labeling by utilizing the consistency of annotated data. We initially create a set of high-quality annotations for a task and then use these annotations to train a parphrasing model, which is subsequently employed to evaluate the consistency of annotated data by determining if two different annotations represent distinct parphrases. If two annotations are not considered parphrases, we assume the original annotations are of high quality. This approach enables the incorporation of quantity control into deep learning models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to five different image segmentation datasets and three text datasets, and the results show it achieves comparable performance to an ideal model with a large quantity of high-quality annotations but requires a significantly smaller amount of actual data.

Creating accurate 2D outdoor terrain maps for robots to navigate is a challenging task, especially in dynamic environments. Most mapping approaches rely on range sensors, are limited to static scenarios, and don't account for forward motion. We present HiTMap, a novel terrain representation that generates detailed 3D maps using a single stereo camera from a mobile platform. Designed to facilitate seamless navigation through forward motion, HiTMap incorporates a unique two-tier structure that maintains a simplified metric map and integrates point clouds based on their proximity to the robot. Our system leverages a motion-correction routine and an adaptive splitting algorithm to ensure accurate mapping in dynamic environments. We demonstrate HiTMap's capabilities, showcasing its application in real-world scenarios and comparing its performance against state-of-the-art 3D mapping algorithms using a variety of evaluation metrics.

Researchers have found that a local magnetic field's effect can be sensitive enough to be detected using atomic interferometry, with limits extending to fields as small as $10^{-17}$ Tesla for a millisecond technique. This achievement enables detection of tiny magnetic fields and could lead to advancements in precision metrology and physics. A novel application of atomic interferometry is presented, utilizing two counter-propagating beams to create a local magnetic field detection system, and demonstrates the technique's effectiveness with argon atoms. A calculation of the detection limits is performed, revealing that they can vary significantly depending on the atomic species used. This discovery demonstrates the versatility of atomic interferometry and showcases the possibility of using it to detect local magnetic fields with extreme sensitivity.

We introduce a new Bayesian nonparametric mixture model where a Dirichlet process prior is placed on densities relative to a given base density, leading to a non-identifiable model when only admixture weights are inferred. We show that by incorporating additional observations or prior information, our approach can recover a non-identifiable model where the admixture weights follow a Dirichlet process prior, enabling us to extract their underlying distribution. Our methodological contributions involve formulating the non-identifiability of a Dirichlet process mixture model and developing a new algorithm to retrieve the underlying Dirichlet process prior. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of simulated scenarios and real-world applications, including the analysis of astrological images and genomic data.

DynaSOAr is a fully dynamic, object-based GPU memory allocator that tackles the limitations of current GPU memory management systems by providing a fast and automatic memory management service for global memory on NVIDIA GPUs.  Our custom DynaSOAr memory allocator features a sophisticated pool-based design, coupled with a cutting-edge, object-aware allocation algorithm, and incorporates sophisticated memory reuse techniques to significantly reduce memory fragmentation and leakage.  We evaluated DynaSOAr's performance in a comprehensive experiment that compared it against three leading GPU memory allocators, along with a benchmark that included 13 real-world object-based GPU applications.  The results showed that DynaSOAr outperformed the competition across the board, achieving a 3.8 times to 11.3 times performance boost and a 5.4 times to 21.3 times speedup in memory allocation and deallocation operations respectively, while also demonstrating improved memory management efficacy, as measured by lower memory fragmentation and leakage rates.

Recently, YSR states have gained significant attention due to their potential to enhance spin-polarization in noble metals. This study delves into the detailed analysis of YSR states induced by magnetic adatoms or dimers on a copper surface, considering the essential spin-orbit coupling in copper. By employing a combined approach of theoretical calculations based on a real-space renormalization group method and scanning tunneling spectroscopy, we obtained precise information about YSR states' energy shifts. Our findings indicate that the spin-orbit coupling significantly affects the YSR states' energy levels, causing shifts of up to 100 meV. This effect becomes more pronounced when two magnetic adatoms form a dimer, leading to a disappearance of the topological edge states and a resultant shift in the peak positions. This discovery implies that the spin-polarization of noble metals can be influenced by the spin-orbit coupling of the surrounding environment.

The Kepler space telescope has enabled the detection of numerous small planets orbiting nearby stars, and by analyzing their transits, researchers have gained valuable insights into the planets' sizes and orbital periods. A notable example is KELT-9b and KELT-4Ab, two planets found to occupy unique positions within their respective stellar systems' habitable zones. Although these planets are gas giants with sizes similar to that of Neptune, their ability to host life is intriguing due to their specific orbital positions. To further understand these planets' characteristics and their host stars, a team of astronomers has conducted a detailed analysis of KELT-9 and KELT-4A through high-resolution spectroscopy and ultraviolet and near-infrared photometry. The resulting data reveal important details about the stars' fundamental properties, as well as the presence of various elements, including the abundance of KELT-9's iron content, which is remarkably high compared to other similar stars. By examining the transital patterns of KELT-9b and KELT-4Ab, the researchers have also derived more precise measurements of their orbital periods, equilibrium temperatures, and tidal interaction characteristics. Additionally, the team has used computer simulations to assess the mini-Neptunes' potential for retaining atmospheres and supporting life forms.

We used computational methods to simulate carbon and nitrogen atoms in different locations within titanium dioxide, specifically in interstitial and substitutional sites. Our analysis showed that, contrary to previous studies, carbon and nitrogen atoms prefer the interstitial sites over substituting for oxygen atoms. Furthermore, we found that these atoms behave as acceptors rather than donors in their site. This unique finding suggests that theoretical models relying on earlier assumptions may require revision.

An analysis at the LHC of the semi-elastic process $pp\to j j j$ is presented, leading to upper limits on four rare decays: $t\to c\mu\gamma$, $t\to c e Z$, $t\to A c$ and $t\to S c$. With 300 $\rm pb^{-1}$ of data at 7 TeV, limits on branching ratios are set at the 10$^{-4}$ level for all four decays. An upgrade to 14 TeV with 300 $\rm pb^{-1}$ of data should lower these limits to the 10$^{-5}$ level.

A key problem in graph theory asks how a given subgraph, which we'll call F, can be colored using the fewest possible colors, while ensuring that no part of F contains a specific substructure known as a triangle with a particular coloring pattern. Researchers have previously established lower bounds for this problem, but only for certain types of subgraphs that contain a triangle. In contrast, a new approach has been developed to tackle subgraphs that don't contain a triangle. Alongside this general solution, a more specific approach is also presented that yields a higher lower bound for triangles itself. In the process, a new concept called the covering edge number of a graph is introduced, offering potential value for graph theory as a whole.

We investigated the sensitivity of different qubit dimensions to measurement errors, specifically qubits and qutrits, in determining their mass. The research considered several error channels, including qubit loss, qutrit collapse, and measurement decoy, and applied a Bayesian approach to calculate the uncertainty of mass measurements. The findings showed that qutrits can tolerate greater noise when attempting to determine their mass than qubits, with qutrits requiring less precise measurements to achieve the same mass accuracy. Furthermore, the optimal measurement decay rates were identified to minimize mass uncertainty under specific error conditions, and the applicability to experimental scenarios was discussed.

The polarization level that can be achieved in positrons is likely a crucial factor for various applications.  We have successfully polarized positrons to a degree greater than 30% for the first time.  This record level of polarization was reached by subjecting a highly polarized beam of electrons to Bremsstrahhlung radiation as they passed through a thin target, converting some of the electrons to positrons.  The polarization of the resulting positron beam was calculated using three different methods.  The level of polarization achieved has significant implications for future research that requires highly polarized positrons.

Let's consider finite groups that reside within a specific family characterized by growing rates of conjugacy classes, nilpotent subgroups, and a polynomial diameter. Our research reveals that within this category, groups with a quadratic or cubic polynomial diameter belong to well-defined classes that include alternating groups, classical matrix groups over finite fields, and certain Lie alchemy groups. Moreover, we demonstrate that groups with a subquadratic polynomial diameter are either non-amenable or possess very specific structures, thereby intersecting with recent findings of Breuillard and Tointon.

A CMOS temperature sensor was created using a single static current mirror and two opamp voltage followers, resulting in a simple and power-efficient design. The sensor exploits the thermal voltage relationship to estimate temperature from a single bias current and the ratio of opamp input and output voltages. Based on a 180nm test chip, the temperature sensor's performance was evaluated through simulation and practical data. Experimental data revealed a mean temperature reading error of 4.5°C and standard deviation of 0.8°C from -20°C to 100°C, across multiple power supply voltages between 0.6V and 1.8V and varying supply noise. The sensor's ability to provide instantaneous reading frequency was demonstrated by applying a step input, revealing a mean time constant of 15.8μs and a sampling rate of 500kSPS. Operational parameters such as reference voltage, absolute temperature reading error, and ratio estimate inaccuracy were analyzed in depth, revealing a mean absolute error of 4.5°C, standard deviation of 0.8°C, mean reference voltage of 820mV, absolute temperature reading error of 2.5°C, and ratio estimate inaccuracy of 0.1%. The test chip's power consumption was found to be 10.3μW at 30mV, enabling the sensor to function within a wide range of environments with high resolution.

We establish a close connection between topological groupoid extensions and certain types of gerbes that are defined over topological stacks. This relationship is made explicit by demonstrating how every topological groupoid extension corresponds to a specific kind of twisted bundle whose underlying space is a topological stack. This generalizes the connection observed in the context of ordinary manifolds. Additionally, we provide criteria for topological groupoid extensions to be equivalent to gerbes over reduced topological stacks. These results are then utilized to illustrate the concept of gerbes in a more accessible manner.

An intriguing relationship exists between massive star formation and the surrounding molecular cores, with many massive star formations located outside the most massive cores.  A statistical analysis of 1214 molecular cores was performed using Australia Telescope Compact Array data to investigate their mass growth and relationships with 86 formed stars.  Results show that the mass growth rate of cores increases with their mass, exhibiting a tendency towards non-linear growth.  Further analysis indicates that cores with formed stars around them tend to have slower mass growth rates compared to those without stars.  A notable observation is that massive star formations are more frequently found in cores with lower mass growth rates rather than the most massive cores.  Aliphatic and sulfur-bearing molecules show increased abundance in cores with formed stars, and massive star formations are more likely to be surrounded by cores enriched in these elements.

A recent result stating that applying differentiation or integration to a zonal function of any type preserves its positive definiteness is incorrect. Contrary to this, we have discovered instances where these operations result in a loss of positive definiteness. Additionally, we have identified specific cases where both differentiation and integration yield functions with which positivity characteristics cannot be determined.

The relationship between foam structure and the flow of its components has been studied, revealing how changes in the size of bubbles affect the viscosity of the foam. By considering the arrangement of bubbles as a key factor, the concept of "roughness factor" was introduced to model their interaction and surface tension. Using this approach, researchers were able to explain how changes in the flow of the foam are influenced by its roughness. By redefining the relationship between stress and strain in the foam, a new model has been developed that incorporates the effects of surface tension and roughness. This model has been applied to a range of experiments where the flow of the foam is subject to different pressures, revealing how the changes in roughness factor affect the flow behavior. Furthermore, by using the model to determine the stress and strain within the foam, researchers were able to define a new measure of roughness that can be used to predict the flow of the foam based on its structure alone.

Deep learning models, specifically convolutional neural networks, have excelled in image classification tasks but come with significant size and training-time limitations for real-world applications.  A pioneering study suggested that ensemble classifiers could effectively address these limitations by achieving superior performance with smaller models.  Building upon this concept, researchers developed a novel ensemble-based convolutional neural network, termed E-CNN, which effectively combines multiple models to achieve a significant reduction in model size and training time.  E-CNN's advantages were demonstrated through comprehensive experiments conducted on three prominent image classification datasets.  Compared to the original model, E-CNN demonstrated improved performance, a notable decrease in model size (average reduction of 89.5%), and a notable decrease in training time (average reduction of 87.5%).  Furthermore, E-CNN exhibited superior performance to traditional ensemble classifiers, showcasing its effectiveness in image classification tasks.

A rotating Hele-Shaw cell with a membraneized gap serves as an intriguing model for studying fluid interface stability, influenced by an externally controllable quantity: membrane tension. By integrating hydrodynamic and surface dynamics equations, our numerical approach allows us to examine the effects of membrane properties on the cell's behavior. Following an initial period of rapid stress buildup, the membrane's behavior can be described by a simplified model exhibiting damped oscillations. As it rotates, the fluid experiences sustained vortex precession, ultimately giving way to a state where a narrow ring of fluid attaches to one wall and rotates above an oil layer. By controlling membrane tension, we found that a specific range enables the fluid ring to stabilize into a long-lived, rotationally stable state. Outside this range, the ring either dissolves or forms a ring that breaks into small droplets.

Cyclopentadiene's CCH to CN abundance ratio shows a clearer 6-fold increase than benzene's ratio following a solar irradiation. This difference is attributed to cyclopentadiene's more even initial distribution of vibrational modes compared to benzene, which allows more effective coupling to solar photons and subsequent degradation processes. As a result, cyclopentadiene exhibits greater reactivity than benzene during solar irradiation, leading to a notable shift in its chemical abundance. This distinction is evident through an analysis of C-H and C-N stretching vibrations expressed as abundance ratios, and can be predicted based on molecular structure, solar spectral energy distribution, and photophysical and photochemical processes. This research provides a detailed case study of a specific molecule, but offers broader implications for understanding the chemical changes induced during solar irradiation, and highlights the importance of considering a molecule's vibrational properties in the context of its environment.

Neural machine translation models have seen significant improvements with the use of attention mechanisms, but these models still suffer from a limitation: they decide what to attend to before knowing what will be translated next. This limitation can lead to suboptimal performance due to the displacement effect, where the model attends to entities that are no longer relevant by the time the corresponding tokens are generated. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a look-ahead attention mechanism that allows the model to take into account the future by attending to ungenerated tokens. We further restrict the look-ahead attention to only consider tokens that have not been generated at a given point, preventing the model from attending to future tokens that have already been generated. We test this mechanism on standard neural machine translation benchmarks and find it to be a useful addition, with the best results achieved by applying it to look-ahead locations that are known in advance. We also test the mechanism on artificial data with varying levels of displacement and find it to be effective in these cases as well.

A translational research approach is being utilized to bridge the gap between engineering and clinical grid computing technologies. This method involves simultaneously conducting fundamental and applied research to develop innovative solutions and apply existing knowledge to create practical applications and infrastructure for grid computing in clinical settings. By taking this translational approach, researchers can leverage the strengths of applied research to drive theoretical developments and guide the evaluation of new methods. This, in turn, enhances the robustness and practical value of their work. A case study involving image registration services is presented to demonstrate the benefits of this approach. This study shows how developing distributed grid services for clinical use drives the creation of new algorithms and cultivates best practices that can be applied to image registration and other medical applications.

To examine the interplay between the $f(R)$ gravity theory and dark matter, researchers modified the $f(R)$ perturbation equation to account for dark matter density fluctuations. By redefining the dark matter density field and using the model's viscosity coefficient, a relation was established that allows $f(R)$ perturbations to evolve in a manner analogous to a dissipative, viscous dark matter system. This formulation enabled the calculation of an effective viscosity coefficient $\chi$ during the early universe stages. By applying this parameter to the $f(R)$ theory, a relation was derived that can be tested against cosmic microwave background data. For the late universe, a connection was made between the viscosity coefficient and a quantity related to the rate of density fluctuation decay, which, in turn, influences the formation of large-scale structures. Given the model's limitations and the need for further analysis of the CMB data, the current findings cannot be validated numerically. However, theoretically, a value of $\chi \approx 10^{-5}$ is expected and has been proposed for future investigation.

Using machine learning, we re-analyzed the full J/	au 	cosmics data from 1.8 to 3.8 GeV in a search for invisible decays. By training a neural network on signal and background events, we obtained a probability distribution for likely signal events. This allows us to set more stringent limits on the cross section for J/	au 	interacting with gluons and dark matter, specifically the effective operator $G \tilde{G} \tilde{S}^2$. With our method, we can set the most stringent limit on the J/	au 	effective operator $G \tilde{G} \tilde{S}^2$ to be less than $1.42 \times 10^{-20}$ GeV$^{-2}$ at 95% confidence, and we suggest this approach for analyzing other J/	au 	datasets.

Multi-scale fractional spectral-sine transformation (MFSSA) is a cutting-edge image decomposition technique that represents images using their sampled properties along certain paths. Originally developed with theoretical purposes in mind, MFSSA can be utilized in various real-world applications and contexts, including the analysis of remote sensing and temperature curve data. This study demonstrates the practical applications of MFSSA by using it to decompose a remote sensing image and a temperature curve from ordinary to high-order fractional representations. Furthermore, MFSSA can be applied to solve an inverse problem related to a non-linear temperature transfer equation.

Let's consider a broad class of random walks with independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) zero-mean increments. We've established conditions under which the asymptotic behavior of these walks is affected by a particular parameter 'b'. If 'b' equals 1, the walks exhibit square-root convergence of their typical path length, yielding an explicit lower bound when 'b' exceeds 1 and an upper bound when 'b' is greater than 2. Our analysis also reveals critical points at 'b' equals 3, 4, 5, and so on, where the asymptotic behavior changes. Furthermore, we apply these findings to study the asymptotic properties of certain stochastic processes that can be reduced to simplified random walk scenarios.

This research focuses on an original plasma source arranged as a coaxial line, which has been used to generate plasmas in various applications requiring optimized parameters such as electron temperature and density. To effectively utilize this source, we developed computational models utilizing two methods: a numerical solution based on finite elements and an analytical approach in a semi-analytical model. Both models yielded comparable results and facilitated further understanding of the source's physics. By applying both models simultaneously, we were able to assess the validity of semi-analytical solutions by comparing them with numerical data. Both models demonstrated comparable accuracy and could be utilized individually to assess the performance of the source or collectively to validate semi-analytical solutions. We utilized both methods to optimize the source's performance by varying key parameters including pressure, power, and gas composition. Utilizing both models, we determined the optimal operating conditions to be 4.5 Pa in pressure, 600 W in power, and a gas composition of 20% oxygen, 40% carbon dioxide, and 40% nitrogen. We also assessed the accuracy of semi-analytical solutions by comparing them with experimental data obtained using a laser interferometer and found them to be reliable.

We propose a novel W-shaped network, combining an U-Net and a FPN, to achieve high efficiency in detecting cells and nuclei in image data. The W-Net surpasses the U-Net and outperforms the FPN by precomputing intermediate feature detection mappings. It shortens detection pathways by inputting already determined features, thereby detecting cells and nuclei more efficiently. The W-Net is applied to the challenging task of detecting nuclei in cytospin images, yielding a 50% reduction in computational cost and a 25% decrease in memory usage while maintaining a 95% detection accuracy comparable to the U-Net.

Let's consider odd special orthogonal groups $SO_{2n+1}(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ and the symplectic group $SP_{2n+1}(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. This research investigates local gamma factors for twisted forms, establishing that rank-one twists suffice to achieve a desired isomorphism of representations. As a result, we can derive rank-one twists that yield equivalent gamma factors, and these twists have explicit relationships with initial twists. Additionally, we can determine if a given twisted form has minimal rank or not. The study further reveals that for $SO_{2n+1}(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ and $SP_{2n+1}(\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$, non-minimal twists arise when the underlying field has a specific property, and we can find the smallest necessary rank to achieve the desired isomorphism of representations.

Recent Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in various tasks but often require large amounts of data to train effectively. We investigate the relationship between traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and fully connected Neural Networks and their equivalent forms in GCNs. By reinterpreting the convolution and fully connected operations within their original spatial or temporal contexts, we derive a fundamental principle that they can be seen as weighted neighborhood aggregation – a key concept underlying GCNs. Leveraging this principle, we develop a novel method to constrain the capacity of GCNs by introducing a regularized form of the graph convolution or fully connected operation, effectively limiting the network's capacity by bounding the weighted neighborhood aggregation. We test this regularized capacity constraint on benchmark datasets MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and Circuits69 and find it yields superior results when the dataset is sufficiently large but also shows an appreciable improvement when applied to smaller datasets like Circuits69.

In this research, we create rotating hairy black holes within pure gravity theory, coupled to a massive scalar field in AdS$_3$, and compare their entropy to standard Chern-Simons theory. We generated metric, conformal factor, and scalar field functions for these hairy black holes through the solution of a system consisting of Einstein's equations, conformal gravity equations, and a massive scalar field equation. We then calculated thermodynamic properties including temperature, entropy, and dimensionless potential, and found that the entropy of these rotating black holes matches that predicted by Chern-Simons theory for pure gravity.

Ultrasound elastography aims to reconstruct tissue stiffness by differentiating tissue axial displacement, which is more distinct than lateral displacement.  This research introduces an axial-limited Differential Elasticity Imaging method that estimates axial elasticity while ignoring lateral details.  A unique algorithm is developed to calculate axial elasticity at multiple depths while accounting for speed variation.  Simulation and phantom tests show that axial-limited elastography accurately replicates actual displacement patterns and facilitates differentiation between hard and soft tissues.  Compared to traditional time-stepping estimation, the proposed method yields greater than 5dB signal-to-noise ratio improvement.  This method's effectiveness is attributed to its ability to bypass the time-stepping algorithm's limitations and accurately estimate speed variation.

Traditional pseudocodes commonly used for algorithmic explanations lack formal logical structure, which can lead to ambiguities and inaccuracies. In contrast, logical pseudocodes utilize mathematical notation to create unambiguous code, ensuring the correctness and safety of algorithms. Despite their benefits, logical pseudocodes are not widely adopted due to the lack of effective tools for writing and verifying them. Our work introduces a novel, type-safe, and formally verifiable pseudocode based on first-order logic, which can be automatically checked for validity and safety guarantees. Our approach also enables the efficient compilation of these pseudocodes into performance-critical algorithms, demonstrating the utility of our approach with a specific example.

We introduce a one-pass algorithm that builds a small subset (coreset) of data points for the $k$-means clustering problem in Euclidean space. This coreset construction takes in the input dataset and cluster centers, and outputs a new set of points whose mean squared distance to given centers is approximately equal to the mean squared distance of the original dataset. As a key contribution, our research reveals that this one-pass coreset construction can be performed with $O(k \cdot d)$ additional dimensions and $O(k^2 \cdot d \cdot \log N)$ storage space, resulting in a significant improvement over prior approaches that required multi-pass constructions or vastly superior approximation factors.

We introduce a new planning approach for large-scale grid worlds by dividing the environment into "superstates," simplifying decision-making by limiting movement between adjacent states. This technique significantly reduces the problem's complexity, enabling efficient solving of large-scale problems. We applied this method to a hypothetical military scenario and found it to be superior to conventional state-based planning.

A theoretical framework that generates partonic distribution functions (PDFs) for W and Z bosons has been developed and applied to evaluate universal corrections to their production Equations. Research reveals that these universal corrections are significant, amounting to 1-3% of the total W or Z boson production, and exhibit a slight dependence on the energy being studied. This discovery prompts data analysts to re-examine the fit process for PDFs, considering the influence of charge asymmetry in the proton and the role of logarithmic corrections from particle interactions. A recommendation is made to utilize modified PDF fit procedures that account for these universal corrections, ensuring more accurate predictions for future experiments at higher energies. A proposal is also made to enhance existing PDF fitting protocols by incorporating new equations that capture the effects of b-quarks on W and Z boson production, which could yield more precise fits when combined with advanced fitting techniques, likely improving the fit's confidence level.

We developed a novel multi-task reinforcement learning algorithm that utilizes multiple dynamics models, one for each task. Each model's primary function is to discover the underlying dynamics and produce policies that maximize rewards in their respective domains. We constrained the models to share a common feature space, which helped prevent overfitting. Our experiments showed that this method achieves better performance than current multi-task learning techniques. We also found that training separate models for each task can sometimes lead to poor results due to model interference, enabling us to highlight this issue and explore ways to address it.

We derive a new form of Godel's first incompleteness theorem that significantly enhances Rosser's 1936 modification of Godel's 1931 first incompleteness theorem. Essentially, any sufficiently powerful formal system with the capacity for arithmetic will contain a specific, universally quantified statement that neither the system itself nor its converse can prove, beyond the capabilities of a diagonalization-based method. This achievement results in a heightened appreciation for the inherent limitations of formal systems in mathematics and highlights the fundamental incompleteness of any attempt to define "provability" within the boundaries of a formal system itself.

This paper provides an interpretation of Hadamard's three circles theorem within the context of monogenic functions in higher dimensional space, revealing it to be a distilled version of a broader theorem applicable to Riemannian manifolds of higher dimensions. The original proof of this theorem, developed by Gelfand and Vilenkin, is then adapted to better suit the underlying geometry of monogenic functions. The resulting theorem is then applied to yield an exact formula for a specific type of linear functional that is comprised of a product of variables raised to specific powers.

We introduce an enhanced conditional Wasserstein GAN, incorporating a regularized term to facilitate the generation of posterior samples. This regularized CWGAN adds a distance term between the generated and target posterior distributions, leading to a benefit of posterior sample generation that can be viewed as inversely beneficial to the mode collapse encountered in traditional WGANS. We leverage this feature to develop a new image generation model, conditioned on a functional observation of a random variable. Our model, Conditional MWGAN, utilizes the posterior sample generator to inversely minimize the regularized conditional Wasserstein distance, resulting in a model that can be trained using observable data. We examine the performance of our model in both synthetic data generation and medical image denoising applications.

This research paper examines the concepts of invariance and stability in fractional order dynamic systems, particularly focusing on subspaces and their relationships. The study begins by presenting definitions of invariant and stable subspaces in the context of fractional order systems. Key findings from the literature are then presented, including the requirement that linear subspaces must satisfy specific conditions to be invariant in fractional order systems. The study also highlights the differences between the stability of subspaces and the invariance of subspaces. The relationship between these subspaces is further explored, along with an examination of the relationships between the Mathtyensens definitions of stability and the corresponding subspaces. The study also explores the relationship between the subspaces defined using the $J$-matrix and the subspaces defined using the Krasnoselskii fixed point theorem. The study concludes by highlighting its contributions to the field, including the introduction of new definitions for the invariance and stability of linear subspaces in fractional order dynamic systems. The study also presents findings that can be applied to the analysis of the stability of fractional order neural networks and the invariance of linear subspaces in fractional order dynamic systems.

Observations of the 39.5-year radio pulse, PSR B1133+16, made over nearly four decades have allowed researchers to isolate and analyze twenty individual scattering screens that pulse's path has encountered. These observations reveal that the outer screen, initially estimated to be 6 to 8 parsecs from Earth, could be as close as 3.8 parsecs and up to 11.8 parsecs based on their respective confidence levels. The tight constraint on the outer screen's distance, coupled with a previously established upper limit, provides the first instance where the screen's distance is constrained below 10 parsecs.

Deep neural networks have effectively modeled complex signals with periodic properties, such as speech, by employing cascaded structures that accommodate time-variant parameters for different frequency components. This research extends the concept to a single-layer neural network, demonstrating that a cascaded network with time-evolving filters can efficiently separate a signal into its constituent frequency bands. A key finding reveals that a time-domain speech signal can be reconstructed from its compressed spectral features using a cascaded network, without requiring any external information. A novel architecture is presented, which incorporates a unique feedback path in each filter module to enhance performance. This research is further supported by an experimental analysis of the cascaded network's performance on both a speech denoising task and a closed-loop speech synthesis system.

We introduce a higher version of topological Hochschild homology (THHH) applicable in bicategorical settings and show it is equivalent to a previously defined concept called shadows. This leads to an interpretation of Poincar\'e duality through THHH, primarily by treating cohomology as a form of homology. Additionally, we find that THHH can be used to extend Witten's twisted K-theory idea to any bicategorical context.

VGG-Sound Source is a comprehensive, freely accessible dataset that represents audio from 345 source categories, compiled using existing datasets and original recordings. Developed to facilitate the development of source-based audio classification models, VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in several key areas. Unlike previous datasets that focus on multi-class audio classification, VGG-Sound Source is designed for all-vs-all classification between its 345 source categories. With over 10 hours of high-quality training data and 1.5 hours of validation data, VGG-Sound Source demonstrates significant progress in source-based audio classification, outperforming models trained on existing datasets by a substantial margin. A key component of VGG-Sound Source is its robust evaluation framework, incorporating multiple sources of bias and innovative methods for reducing their impact through dataset mixing and reinforcement learning. When put to use, these methods help mitigate bias and enhance model performance on unseen data, as confirmed by our experiments. We have made VGG-Sound Source available through the following link: https://datascience.vgg.ntua.gr/VGG-Sound-Source-Dataset.

Previous work on graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in hyperbolic space has focused on generalizing Euclidean GCNs, leading to increased computational complexity and memory usage. This has limited their applicability in large-scale graph analytics. Our novel Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) surpasses existing hyperbolic GCNs by providing a more efficient solution, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art hyperbolic GCNs while significantly reducing computational complexity and memory usage. Specifically, LGCN boasts $O(n^2d)$ time and $O(md + n^2)$ space complexities compared to $O(n^3d)$ and $O(nd + n^3)$ for existing hyperbolic GCNs, where $n$ represents the number of data points, $d$ is the graph signal dimension, and $l$ is a hyperbolic manifold dimension that typically remains low. We further enhance LGCN's performance by introducing a Lorentzian graph convolutional unit (LGCU) and incorporating a geometric-based pooling method, resulting in an improved LGCN (iLGCN). Experimentation on synthetic data and real-world datasets reveals that LGCN and iLGCN outperform state-of-the-art hyperbolic GCNs in terms of node classification accuracy, especially in large-scale graphs.

This work presents an alternative proof of a recent stability estimate in a specific inverse problem, which involves determining a coefficient of an anisotropic heat equation based on boundary measurements. Originally established by Delay and Rosnals, our approach simplifies their proof and utilizes a distinct strategy. We begin by utilizing an existing observability inequality to establish an unstable inverse method, then employ it to obtain a strong stability estimate in the $H^{-1}$ norm. By combining this with an existing regularity result and the finite-dimensional manifold approach, we can solve the problem.

A Tsallis distribution can be reinterpreted within a social framework by considering agents with varying levels of success who then take part in new interactions based on relative performance, effectively leading to generalized exponential behavior.

To analyze the effects of a mass term on the degrees of freedom within a linearized gravity theory, consider gravitational perturbations defined as deviations from a background metric in an arbitrary static electromagnetic field. By applying a Fierz-Pauli type mass term to the 5-dimensional AdS space, we observed that a degree of freedom is missing compared to similar analyses in $4D$ and $5D$ without a mass term. Furthermore, by switching to a conformally coupled Fierz-Pauli type mass term in the $5D$ AdS space, we found that an additional degree of freedom appears and the missing degree of freedom found in the $4D$ AdS space remains absent. Both of these cases result in unique Bunch-Dolgov and Boulton-Hsu parameterizations. Additionally, we derived the linearized gravity equations with a mass term and showed that they admit exact solutions, which can be used to the 5-dimensional AdS space, mimicking the 4-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet scenario and to a 4-dimensional conformally coupled Fierz-Pauli type mass term with a massless graviton.

A mathematical framework for executing Hamiltonian dynamics on quantum systems has been established, yet the underlying theory remains underdeveloped. In contrast to its classical counterpart, the scope of quantum Hamiltonian dynamics is unclear due to multiple definitions competing for equivalence. We have discovered that previous results can be refined by categorizing all quantum Hamiltonian dynamics into four distinct groups, each with its own defining characteristics. These categories differ significantly in their logical connections to quantum equilibrium states and correlated observables. As a result, researchers must approach claims related to quantum Hamiltonian dynamics with a critical eye, being aware that many results actually apply to specific subcategories rather than the general concept.

A two-level system can be thought of as being analogous to a spinning top, and both of these can be described using quantum mechanics. We'll examine how this two-level system can be visualized as being made up of two spinning tops that are independent of one another. This leads to a definition of negative temperature that can be easily illustrated using the tops' relative spin velocities. It can take on both positive and negative values, representing them as opposing directional arrows on a number line. It's essential to note that this concept of negative temperature isn't unique to the two-level system and can be applied to any multi-level system. It's also worth pointing out that it's not possible to achieve a negative temperature in the spinning top system if it consists of multiple independent tops, and the same rule applies to the two-level system and any other system with independent energy levels.

This research investigates a type of minimal dark sector that interacts with neutrinos, utilizing a seesaw framework to stabilize the vacuum while maintaining dark parity symmetry, and it incorporates a mechanism to address the dark parity violation problem. By defining a minimal dark parity invariant Lagrangian and identifying the minimal dark parity violating terms that prevent the vacuum from becoming unstable, it can be determined how a minimal dark sector affects the neutrino oscillation parameters. Furthermore, the condition for avoiding a conflict with the observed value of the muon anomalous magnetic moment is established. The findings can be applied to both the singlet and triplets of a minimal dark sector.

To understand the behavior of transition metal oxides, it's crucial to consider both their spin-orbit interaction and crystal field splitting. However, these two energies often vary significantly, leading researchers to analyze a system's dynamics by framing the spin-orbit interaction in terms of either fluctuating electrons or frozen ions. Most studies have focused on either the strong or weak coupling limit, but our work delves into the intermediate range where crystal field splitting surpasses spin-orbit interaction. By applying a multi-configuration impurity model, we were able to assess the impact of interactions and find that they induce an effective spin-orbit coupling that aligns with either the original or opposite direction of the initial condition, depending on the degree of electron delocalization. Notably, we observed that the anti-ferroelectric behavior characteristic of some transition metal oxides can arise from local field effects rather than dipolar interactions. Finally, we applied our research to the specific case of BaTiO3, a well-known anti-ferroelectric material, and found that its properties might be influenced more significantly by the spin-orbit interaction than previously thought.

This research focuses on examining the properties of relative $I$-functions associated with toric complete intersections that have smooth divisors.  Toric complete intersections with smooth divisors serve as key objects of study in this research, and it has been discovered that those with a specific level of simplicity possess unique $I$-functions that are interrelated in a specific manner.  Furthermore, it has been found that the relative $I$-functions of these toric complete intersections can be expressed in terms of a specific $I$-function arising from the hypergeometric series, and the nature of these $I$-functions has been explored through the study of algebraic functions.  Additionally, the research develops relationships between the $A$-hypergeometric systems and the $D$-modules of toric local rings, and it introduces an algebraic approach to analyzing the properties of relative $I$-functions.

Our investigation highlights how affecting latent code in medical image GANs influences the interpretation of ME images. We discovered that altering specific latent code components could artificially create abnormalities in normally healthy images. This phenomenon raised concerns about the potential for misdiagnosis. We propose a straightforward method to ensure healthcare professionals are aware of this potential risk. This approach involves providing healthcare professionals with an interactive tool that allows them to manipulate latent code and see the effects on ME images. We used this tool to conduct an experiment on Radiologist-measured ME image alterations. The results showed that manipulating latent code could lead to incorrect diagnoses. We also found that certain code components consistently produced abnormalities even when used alone. We believe that future medical image generation techniques must consider this finding and develop methods to prevent latent code from inducing conditions in healthy images. We have made our code and data available at https://github.com/zhong-jian-yang/LatentCodeMedicalImages.

ViDaExpert is an interactive data visualization tool designed to simplify the exploration of large datasets with multiple dimensions. It allows users to easily navigate complex data by creating interactive 3D projections and combining them with 2D representations, and it includes a feature to identify data points within the visualizations. ViDaExpert can be utilized through a user-friendly web interface, and it has been utilized in an assessment of a course management system used by over 500 students. The system included over 100,000 entries with 15 attributes, and it served as a large-scale test case to validate the effectiveness of ViDaExpert. The validation process involved conducting a user study with 11 participants who were asked to locate specific entries within the system using ViDaExpert, and the results showed a significant decrease in search time as users became more experienced with the tool.
